A detailed analysis of this latent space allows for the clear identification and separation of specific regimes, including: (a) the clear contrast between stable conditions and deep convection defined by low longwave radiation and strong precipitation; (b) the segregation of high thin-featured cirrus clouds from thick, low-elevation cirrus types (note: *correcting source ambiguity to "optically thick"*); and (c) the linkage of shallow convection to large-scale moisture levels and surface heating. Sorting the states of an automaton in accordance with some prior ordering of the base alphabet is a foundational approach to computing properties of the accepted language. A key development in this area involves Wheeler graphs, which extend the Burrows-Wheeler Transform—from its origins in strings—to graph-structures. These graphs represent a vital data structure for languages because of their efficient storage for automaton transitions alongside rapid handling of various substring queries. This efficiency stems from a defining property called \emph{path coherence}, which relies on a node ordering that extends to sets of paths. Interpreting an ordered Wheeler graph as itself an automaton reveals that the resulting string ordering follows the reverse lexicographic order associated with strings entering any given state. This observation invites the analysis of the "Wheeler" class of regular languages. Unlike general cases, the powerset construction method for deterministic conversion runs in polynomial time specifically for these Wheeler languages. This property renders numerous standard language decision problems tractable in polynomial time, and it allows for poly-time solutions regarding whether a given NFA accepts a Wheeler language or whether a resulting DFA possesses Wheeeler properties. This paper establishes an upper bound on this simplicity: relaxing the constraints, such as allowing standard non-ordered NFAs, transforms many of these previously easy tasks into computationally complex problems that become NP-complete or PSPACE-complete.

Two-view knowledge graphs (KGs) unify two distinct perspectives: an upper layer ontology view handling abstract, common-sense ideas, and an instance view detailing specific entities derived from those concepts. Consequently, these models possess a hybrid structure, characterized by hierarchy in the ontology view and cyclicality in the instance view. However, most recent embedding approaches treat entire KGs as belonging to only a single structural type. Even when previous methods attempt to integrate both views within a shared geometry (e.g., Euclidean or non-Euclidean product spaces), this approach becomes theoretically unsuitable as distinct sections of the graph inherently possess different structural properties. To solve these limitations, we introduce and implement a dual-geometric space embedding model (DGS) based on complex non-Euclidean geometry, which assigns unique geometric spaces to different portions of the graph. This model integrates hyperbolic space, spherical space, and an intersecting conceptual space within a cohesive learning framework. Specifically for spherical space, we developed novel operations that function directly within the spherical domain, eliminating the requirement for approximate tangent space projections. Empirical results on public datasets demonstrate that the DGS substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in KG completion tasks, confirming its efficacy in capturing diverse structural characteristics within two-view knowledge graphs.

We investigate phase and thermal conductivity in T-shaped uncorrelated double-quantum-dot Josephson junctions using the Keldysh non-equilibrium Green's function formalism. Split learning serves as a distributed training approach enabling multiple entities to collaboratively build a machine learning model using vertically partitioned datasets divided by attribute. Moreover, our results indicate that TPSL achieves a superior balance between privacy preservation and model utility when compared to established baselines.

Soft actuators provide a secure yet versatile solution for activities requiring delicate graspng and agile manipulation, though developing precise models for these systems is difficult because their deformable materials obey complex physics. We integrated the model into predictive controllers which required less computational iterations than traditional methods including reinforcement actor-critic, PD controllers etc., proving their efficiency over other algorithms used in motion control systems.

This study analyzes circadian patterns of subscribers in Budapest, Hungary, by processing mobile Call Detail Records (CDR). This research presents an operator derivation for multiple Boris algorithms based on a rigorous analysis of trajectory errors within a constant magnetic field. Such errors—specifically concerning gyroradius offsets—and discrepancies in particle location, serve as the core reasons the original Boris solvers were developed, detached from finite-difference frameworks. The study reveals that exactly two independent strategies exist to eliminate these errors and ensure perfect adherence to the cyclotron orbit: one recovers the recognized second-order symmetric Boris solver, while the second uncovers a previously unrecognized on-orbit solution unattainable via traditional finite-difference methods. Re-examination of earlier literature highlights a common conflation between a problematic, inferior leapfrog Boris variant and its superior second-order symmetric counterpart, the latter of which maintains significantly higher accuracy. In combined, non-uniform electric and magnetic fields, the trajectory of this latter solver stays proximate to the actual cyclotron orbit even when time steps exceed the cyclotron period. Finally, the operator framework demonstrates Buneman's cycloid fitting technique as mathematically equivalent to Boris' on-orbit solution, rendering Boris' standard splitting of velocity parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field redundant.

Although monocular 3D object detection has progressed substantially through the adoption of pre-trained depth estimators for pseudo-LiDAR recovery, these conventional two-stage approaches often struggle with overfitting and fail to explicitly represent the geometric link between object bounding boxes and depth. To address these issues, we introduce OPA-3D, a single-stage, end-to-end, Occlusion-Aware Pixel-Wise Aggregation network that simulates jointly predicting dense scene depth, depth-bounding box deviations, and object locations to achieve robust two-stream 3D detection. Specifically, the Geometry Stream integrates observed depth and bounding box residue estimates to recover object boundaries using explicit occlusion-aware optimization. Concurrently, a bounding box-based geometric projection strategy supports improved distance estimation, while the Context Stream directly regresses the object's spatial extent and position. This dual-stream architecture additionally allows for the enforcement of cross-stream consistency, aligning both branches to enhance overall results. Comprehensive evaluations on public benchmarks show that OPA-3D outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions on key vehicle categories with maintained real-time performance. All training configurations and code will be made publicly available shortly.

Although machine learning algorithms serve many prediction purposes, they risk learning patterns that discriminate against sensitive attributes like gender or race. This manuscript presents the R package 'fairadapt', a pre-processing technique rooted in causal inference. The study of ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems hinges fundamentally on irreducibility. As seen in the literature, results addressing the irreducibility of Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) and Stochastic Partial Differential Equations (SPDEs) under purely jump noise remain scarce. Current methodologies primarily mimic those used for Gaussian settings and depend heavily on specific characteristics of additive noise, specifically its resemblance to stable processes. Furthermore, applying these conventional methods to alternative additive jump noise types is problematic, and the scenario of multiplicative noise appears entirely intractable using such approaches. This paper introduces a novel and efficient framework to establish the irreducibility for SPDEs and SDEs driven by multiplicative pure jump noise. The constraints imposed on coefficients and noise are minimal—effectively approaching necessity—and sufficient. Consequently, this work significantly advances upon existing literature by demonstrating new irreducibility properties for a broad spectrum of pure jump noise-driven equations, under conditions far weaker than those required by prior methods. Our main results apply directly to diverse problems including locally monotone coefficients in SPDEs, cases involving singular coefficients in SPDEs and SDEs, nonlinear Schrödinger and Euler equations, among others. Importantly, within this framework, compound Poisson processes may serve as the driving noise, and they are capable of being infinite-dimensional—an aspect we consider unexpected.

**Objective:** Although the Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) score, derived from CT scans, serves as a robust and independent marker for coronary heart disease (CHD) events, its clinical utility is hindered by limited inter-scan reproducibility. To address this, we introduce a threshold-independent method for CAC quantification. **Methods:** This approach employs a Generative Adversarial Network (specifically CycleGAN) to de-compose images containing CAC into separate components representing background tissue and isolated calcifications. Inter-scan reproducibility was evaluated in 1,662 patients undergoing paired scan comparisons using 676 planning CTs. **Outcomes:** The proposed technique demonstrated superior reproducibility with an average inter-scan CAC mass difference of 47%, markedly lower than the 89% seen in standard manual calcium scoring, and yielded an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient of 0.96 for Agatston scores versus 0.91 for automatic clinical scoring. **Conclusions:** By significantly improving inter-scan reproducibility, this method offers the potential for more accurate long-distance risk stratification and refined precision in predicting future coronary heart disease.

To ensure reliability in real-world applications, machine learning techniques must handle input samples that do not conform to their training distributions (out-of-distribution or OOD). Although existing solutions primarily focus on detecting these anomalies to flag uncertain inputs for the user, such methods often fail to provide clarity. When OOD inputs significantly resemble training data, simple yes-or-no anomaly indicators lack explainability. Consequently, we present a novel hierarchical approach where prediction granularity dynamically adjusts as input ambiguity increases. By moving toward broader, more conservative classifications under high uncertainty—for instance, categorizing an unknown bird as simply "bird" rather than outright "OD"—this method delivers richer information to users compared to strict binary flags. Furthermore, evaluating performance at each hierarchy layer enhances both interpretability and explainability. Finally, our research confirms the efficacy of these hierarchical models in tackling OOD problems requiring both fine and coarse-grained detection levels.

We present the initial experimental proof of strange nonchaotic attractor (SNA) occurring in the natural dynamics of an autonomous, self-oscillating laboratory system. Although prior investigations identified SA generation only within quasiperiodically forced regimes, this study provides the long-overdue evidence of SNA within a standalone experimental setup. We observed the emergence of SNA between periodic and chaotic states via fractalization using a lab-scale thermoacoustic system, and validated the chaotic transition through a range of established nonlinear diagnostics for confirming SNA.

We introduce a route choice model that characterizes traveler behavior as a flow allocation maximizing utility across the whole network subject to flow conservation, with substitution driven by route overlap. The model estimates behavior for all available alternatives simultaneously, eliminating the need for choice set generation. Estimation relies solely on linear regression, enabling high computational speed. Furthermore, model predictions via convex optimization are easily computed, even for large-scale network scenarios, facilitating straightforward application. We validate this approach using extensive data comprising 1,337,096 GPS trip records from the Greater Copenhagen road network.

This paper introduces Sequential Aggregation and Rematerialization (SAR), a distributed algorithm for full-batch Graph Neural Network (GNN) training across large-scale graphs. While recent large-scale GNN efforts largely rely on sampling or non-differentiable message-passing techniques, SAR enables direct distributed training of any GNN architecture using complete large graphs. SAR introduces a distributed sequential rematerialization strategy that re-computes and subsequently releases specific sections of the excessively large GNN computational graphs during backward passes. This approach yields superior memory scalability, reducing memory usage per compute node proportionally with the number of workers, even in densely connected datasets. Leveraging SAR, the researchers achieve the largest-scale full-batch GNN training applications known to date, demonstrating that expanding the number of workers drastically reduces memory consumption. Additionally, the authors propose a general optimization technique based on kernel fusion and attention-matrix rematerialization to simultaneously enhance runtime and memory efficiency in attention-based models; integrated with SAR, these custom kernels deliver notable improvements in speed and memory utilization for such architectures. We have released the SAR library for GNN training, available at https://github.com/IntelLabs/SAR.

The performance of the LHCb experiment's Ring-imaging Čerenkov (RICH) detectors is evaluated using LHC Run 2 data from 2015 to 2018 during operation. This analysis measures how the resolution stability of the Cherenkov angle and the fluctuations in detected photon count evolve over time under different running conditions. Furthermore, when particle identification capabilities are benchmarked against real detector data, they are confirmed to meet all necessary requirements for the experiment's scientific objectives.

This study addresses the challenges of model pre-training and designing reusable backbones for downstream tasks. This study presents key advances in automatic lyrics transcription. The primary contribution is MSTRE-Net, a unique extension of the Multistreaming Time-Delay Neural Network architecture, which utilizes multiple parallel processing streams with diverse time resolutions. Maintained at lower computational volume, MSTRE-Net enables quicker inference and superior recognition performance compared to architectures employing only uniformly spaced TDNN streams. Complementarily, we introduce two innovative preprocessing procedures: utilizing a combined dataset from mono‑ and polyphonic sources to enhance an acoustic model and introducing distinct markers to monophonic and polyphonic material to aid the alignment of music-only intervals against vocal silences. We further provide a substantially newer test collection with broader genre variation and increased item counts relative to prior benchmarks, while ensuring parity in singer demographics to maximize fairness in lyrics decoding tasks via the best performance model. All experimental identifiers and resources required for the reproducible research are now made public via code and data identifiers for sharing with our academic community.

Virol.* {\bf 92}, e01522-17 (2018)] to exhibit self-propagated rolling across glycan-coated surfaces. Building upon our prior proposal that these spiky attachment enzymes cut sugars to function as self-organized mechano-chemical systems [F. Ziebert and I. M. Kuli\'{c}, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* {\bf 126}, 218101 (2021)], the present work provides a more comprehensive physical analysis of this emergent self-rolling phenomenon. We establish scaling laws describing the generation of this motion, complemented by an analytical framework that determines the full force-torque and rotational velocity profiles of this actuation. To test our findings, stochastic Gillespie simulations confirm the model and measure probabilistic occurrences such as virus separation from the surface or changes in rolling direction. Furthermore, the study re-validates prior assumptions in light of current results and confirms that the mechanism remains highly robust. Ultimately, this convergence of findings indicates that viral rolling driven by localized enzymatic action is the statistical majority outcome rather than the exception.

Angluin's L\* algorithm constructs the minimal, complete Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) for a regular language by utilizing membership and equivalence queries. Its Probabilistically Approximately Correct (PAC) variant reduces equivalence queries to a substantial number of random membership queries to achieve high reliability in answers. Consequently, this method is adaptable to any device, regular or not, and functions as an automata synthesizer that abstracts a device's behavior through observation. This work analyzes the behavior of the PAC learning process applied to devices generated from DFAs through various noise introductions. Specifically, it investigates the algorithm's capacity to reduce noise and produce a DFA closer to the original source than the original noise configuration. Three distinct noise models are proposed: (1) the device classifies words with a small inversion probability, (2) the device randomly alters input letter sequences before querying, and (3) the device combines classifications from both the DFA and an automata counter. Experiments involved hundreds of DFAs. Our primary contributions demonstrate bluntly that: (1) the algorithm operates effectively when noise arises from random processes; (2) it performs inadequately in the presence of structured noise; and (3) with near-certainty, these randomized processes generate systems possessing non-recursively enumerable languages.

Scheduled sampling effectively mitigates the exposure bias inherent in Neural Machine Translation by simulating an inference environment where ground-trution tokens are randomly replaced with model predictions during training. Although successful, this method relies solely on training steps to determine scheduling intervals, overlooking the model's real-time proficiency and thereby constraining its performance ceiling and convergence velocity. To overcome these limitations, we introduce confidence-aware scheduled sampling, which measures contemporary model competence via prediction confidence to establish fine-grained sampling strategies. Consequently, high-confidence positions receive predicted tokens, mimicking inference conditions more closely for those instances while retaining ground-trth data at low-confidence positions which remain difficult. Additionally, we observe that traditional scheduled sampling often degrades back into standard teacher-forcing modes since many predicted tokens coincide with ground truth; addressing this within our confidence-aware framework, we deliberately expose a greater variety of noise, including word repetition and syntactical errors alongside predicted tokens, for locations where the confidence is actually quite high. Validation conducted on Transformers using large-scale WMT benchmarks (WMT 2014 EN–DE/FR and WMT 2019 ZH–EN) demonstrates that our proposed strategy substantially surpasses both the standard Transformer baseline and conventional scheduled sampling in both final translation quality and convergence rates.

We utilized Fisher-Shannon (FS) analysis to examine 1-hour frequency wind time series collected vertically from 1.5 to 25.5 meters in an urban setting. As a established tool for characterizing the intricacy of nonlinear systems, the FS method evaluates order-to-disorder transitions within time series data. Our results indicate a decline in FS complexity—which results from the combination of Shannon entropy power and the Fisher Information Measure—as anemometer height increases. This suggests a distinct vertical dependence on the ordering dynamics of high-frequency wind speeds in cities. Additionally, the relationship between wind size metrics and the daily variance of local temperatures mirrors this vertical trend; the correlation is significantly stronger at lower levels, underscoring the critical role of surface temperature fluctuations in driving near-ground wind variability.

In numerous classification models, transforming data into discrete bins enhances distribution estimation. Traditional discretization strategies often prioritize maximizing discriminator power rather than improving classification generalization. Consequently, this leads to excessive fragmentation where data are split into numerous tiny bins, as continuous un-binned data retains maximum discriminant signal. To address this, we introduce a Max-Dependency-Min-Divergence (MDmD) criterion designed to simultaneously optimize the generalization capability inherent in both discriminant strength. Specifically, the Max-Dependency (MDM) component maximizes the statistical relationship between classified variables and discretized input features, whereas the Min-Divergence component explicitly reduces the Jenson-Shannon divergence between training and validation sets under a fixed partition scheme. Although the MDmD approach is theoretically promising, reliably estimating high-order joint probability distributions remains a significant hurdle. To overcome this practical challenge, we propose a Max-Relevance-Min-Divergence (MRmD) scheme that discretizes attributes independently. This approach balances maximizing relevance and ensuring robustness across training and validation sets. Experimental evaluations against cutting-edge discretization methods within a naive Bayes framework, utilizing 45 machine learning benchmark datasets, demonstrate that the proposed MRmD method substantially outperforms existing approaches in most scenarios.

Although conversation ubiquitously features disfluencies, this phenomenon remains an under-examined area within natural language processing (NLP), predominantly because suitable datasets have historically been scarce. To address this, we introduce Disfl-QA, a new challenge question answering dataset derived from SQuAD, in which human contributors insert contextual disfluencies into originally fluid questions. This dataset encompasses various difficult forms of disfluencies that necessitate a deeper textual comprehension compared to earlier resources. Experimental findings indicate that existing state-of-the-art question answering systems experience substantial performance degradation when evaluated on Disfl-QA without prior exposure to disfluencies. We present methods based on data augmentation to mitigate potential accuracy losses and also illustrate the effectiveness of fine-tuning with gold-standard labeled data. We contend that robust NLP models rely on large-scale datasets containing disfluencies; our resources, which are publicly hosted at https://github.com/google-research-datasets/disfl-qa, represent a significant step in achieving this robustness.

This study performs a comprehensive evaluation of automatic hate speech (HS) detection, employing various state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines across 6 datasets to complete 11 specific subtasks. Our primary motivation is to ascertain whether recent SOTA models serve as the optimal choice for HS detection, and if techniques such as data augmentation and ensembling further enhance their performance. Additionally, we execute six cross-task experiments. Our results establish new SOTA records on two subtasks—achieving 91.73% and 53.21% macro F1 scores on HASOC 2020's subtasks A and B, which represent a significant improvement upon previous SOTA figures of 51.52% and 26.52%, respectively. On two further datasets, we attain performance nearing SOTA levels: recording macro F1 scores of 81.66% on OLID 2019's subtask A (SOTA: 82.9%)-and 82.54% on HASOC 2021 subtask A (SOTA: 83.05%). We conduct an error analysis and employ explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) tools—specifically IG and SHAP—to illustrate the decision-making processes of the Bi-LSTM and T5 models using representative examples. Further contributions include: (1) introducing a simple yet innovative method to rectify out-of-class predictions in T5; (2) providing a detailed account of data augmentation techniques; (3) uncovering poor data annotations within HASOC 2021 through illustrative cases and XAI, thereby highlighting the necessity for superior data quality control; and (4) openly releasing our model checkpoints and code to support research transparency.

The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is an evolving research domain that leverages global Internet connectivity to transform ordinary objects into autonomous smart devices. Beyond their applications in smart homes and urban environments, these services are integral to the Philosophy of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, often cited as the cornerstone of the "Industry 4.0" concept. Embracing IIoT allows established sectors to streamline production, cut operational expenses, and boost overall industrial efficiency. Nevertheless, the integration of diverse hardware, reliance on third-party solutions, and the limited resources typical of IoT endpoints introduce novel security hazards within the supply chain, creating new vulnerabilities. Consequently, certain threats, such as Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks, pose significant threats. This paper examines these specific dangers, highlighting the adverse effects of DDOs on manufacturing workflows and the communication integrity of related applications. To combat these issues, we propose a comprehensive security framework; by drawing on the benefits of fog computing, this architecture demonstrates scalable counter-measures and provides strategic approaches for effectively deploying DDO mitigation techniques across vast installations.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) involves hydrodynamical processes requiring swift gas cooling; it is posited to function in the outer sectors of protoplanetary disks. Although the VSI generates vertical turbulent motions capable of influencing dust accumulation and sinking, dust dynamics can conversely dampen the instability: reduced gas opacity due to dust removal hampers cooling in the already thin outer regions. Utilizing linear analysis, this research quantifies how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. By devising a cooling timescale model that accounts for dust maturation beyond one micron and size-dependent sedimentation, we integrate it with linear stability analysis to determine VSI activity regions (the "VSI zones") and their peak growth rates at various radii. Results indicate that dust maturation and sinking confine the VSI zone more tightly along the midplane, resulting in reduced growth rates due to diminished shear in the vertically weaker velocity fields near the lower disk altitudes. Specifically, for a 0.01 solar mass disk, allowing dust to grow from 10 microns to 1 mm suppresses growth rates by an order of magnitude exceeding 10. Consequently, dust-driven turbulence suppression likely facilitates additional outer-disk dust evolution and accounts for the pronounced settling seen in the HL Tau system.

Mispurchasing medication can lead to unforeseen and hazardous patient outcomes, posing a significant safety risk. In order to mitigate this possibility, we have created an automated framework capable of identifying prescriptions derived from mobile-captured images of pills. Central to this work is a specialized pill-preservation matching task, designed to align the visible pill photographs within images against the corresponding drug names listed in their prescriptions. Building on this, we present a new solution called PIMA that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and contrastive learning methodologies. Specifically, the GNN component captures the positional relationships among text fields in digital prescriptions to isolate those segments that contain pill identifiers, while the application of contrastive learning fosters a deeper understanding of the simillarity structures across two different modalities: visual pill impressions and their textual counterparts. Through broad empirical validation involving experiments on an authentic, custom-assembled dataset of prescription document and pill photos, PIMA was found to significantly surpass existing model baselines—increasing classification accuracy from just under 19.1% to nearly 47. We posit that these developments will pave new pathways for clinically beneficial tools designed to enhance overall medication safety and refine the standard of patient care and support.

Transfer learning seeks to improve target task performance by capitalizing on knowledge embedded within pre-trained models. While earlier approaches primarily focused on selecting a single source model, the rise of deep networks has created vast repositories containing models of diverse architectures, training data, and learning strategies known as model hubs. Applying standard single-source transfer methods to every model in such hubs not only wastes this collective knowledge but also incurs significant computational overhead. This study introduces the **Hub-Pathway framework**, designed to orchestrate learning directly from a model hub. Core components generate data-driven weights to determine input-level pathways, selectively activating and routing specific models, followed by output-level aggregation that combines these predictions. Trained end-to-end using the target task's objective function, the framework dynamically learns optimal structural configurations tailored for individual input data, maximizing the utility of available pre-trained models. Furthermore, a noisy pathway generator coupled with an exploration loss is employed to encourage the discovery of varied routes. Additionally, each model is fine-tuned on specialized, activating data subsets, ensuring robustness while optimizing overall knowledge transfer. Empirical evaluations across vision and reinforcement learning domains confirm that the Hub-Pathway framework establishes state-of-the-art performance standards for model hub transfer learning.

Driven by the realization that the phenomenological treatment of optical activity in chiral media by Fresnel is inconsistent, we performed an extensive examination of plane wave polarization. Surprisingly, this quasi-spin is non-observably defined within a laboratory framework but rather applies relative to a momentum-specific local reference frame. Its corresponding mathematical operators mirror Pauli matrices. Similarly to the Jones vectors representing the state function describing polarization, fully defining the polarization state demands two distinct sets of degrees of freedom: one set characterizing the quasi-spin itself (manifested by the expectation values of Pauli operators known as Stokes parameters, projected onto a state defined by the Jones matrix) and the second specifying the local coordinate system (covering propagation orientation an angle of rotational reference). Consequently, polarization evolves through two independent mechanisms: altering the internal quasi-spin while holding the reference frame constant (the traditional approach, expressed via an $\mathrm{SU(2)}$ rotation of the Jones matrix) or adjusting the reference frame while the internal quasi-spin remains invariant within it. Ultimately, it is this recently identified second mechanism responsible for explaining the phenomenon of optical activity.

Over recent decades, Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) forces have garnered significant research interest owing to their critical role in spectroscopic predictions and geometry optimization. This study evaluates the precision and computational expenses associated with these forces. We implement the zero-bias zero-bias (ZVZB) force estimator across standard and diffusion Monte Carlo frameworks, employing mean-field trial wavefunctions and atomic pseudopotentials. To determine statistical force uncertainties in the context of heavily tailed QMC data, we applied a novel regression method previously detailed by P. Lopez Rios and G. J. Conduit. Our analysis, covering selected atoms and diatomic molecules from hydrogen (Z = 1) to zinc (Z = 20), examines how both accuracy and computational burden evolve as effective pseudopotential valence charge ($Z_{|\rm eff$}) rises. Our findings indicate that the cost of calculating both QMC energies and forces scales according to approximate power laws with respect to $Z_{|\rm eff$). Specifically, force uncertainties increase more quickly than energies, resulting in a scaling requirement near $Z_{|\rm eff}^{6.5(3)}$ for Diffusion Monte Carlo. Furthermore, we observe that feasible system sizes scale inversely with $Z_{|\rm eff}^2$. Notably, this trend holds regardless of underlying model assumptions or the application of "space warp" variance reductions in diffraction calculations. These results forecast the practical limitations of acquiring QMC forces across various material classes, including transition metal oxides, where such force evaluations are currently absent; this deficiency further highlights the urgent need for advanced variance reduction strategies within QMC methodologies, particularly those addressing atoms with elevated $Z_{|\rm eff}^2$.

Disentangled black hole microstates represent rare configurations in holographic CFTs because they correspond to gravity solutions that lack smooth horizons. We argue that an abundance of these states exists within the microcanonical spectrum such that nearly all of these states lack horizons, allowing any generic microstate to be rewritten as a superposition of horizonless ones; in fact, the semi-classically accessible entropy suggests that almost total black hole Bekenstein–Hawking entropy can be realized in this way. Furthermore, in generic quantum systems with short-range interactions, the microcanonical thermodynamic entropy is overwhelmingly dominated by area-law eigenstates in the large-volume (thermodynamic) limit. Since entangled volume-law dominance characterizes typical quantum states, the prevalence of area-law configurations in this context is a distinct exception. We explicitly demonstrate a class of area-law unit vectors (constructed via a GNS-GLR type approach) such that each state's conditional mutual information is proportional to its boundary area rather than its volume, and suggest that an analogous construction method likely applies to black hole microstates as well.

This paper investigates the translational and rotational dynamics of neutrally-buoyant spheroids of finite size suspended in hydrodynamic turbulence using comprehensive numerical simulations. The study covers axisymmetric configurations ranging from oblate to prolate shapes across different particle volumes. Findings indicate that while non-spherical particles at the inertial scale encounter accelerated and rotated states due to volume-filtered fluid forces and torques—mirroring observations in spherical particles—the orientation of non-spheres exhibits specific signatures. These signatures reveal preferential alignments with adjacent flow structures, manifesting in differing axial and lateral fluctuation patterns in acceleration and angular rates. Furthermore, random reorientation of non-spheres does not materialize, even for inertial range equivalent diameters reaching 60 $\eta$ when $Re_{\lambda}=120$. Finally, the analysis demonstrates that excluding hydrodynamic boundary layers formed around particles prevents a quantitatively accurate description of their statistical dynamics, particularly regarding the magnitude of angular velocities and the distinction between tumbling and spinning motion. Overall, this work underscores the pivotal role inertial-scale flow structures play in the transport of neutrally-buoyant bodies of finite size relative to homogeneous and isotropic turbulent flows.

Furthermore, geometric TDI offers an intuitive physical framework for interpreting the synthesis of virtual optical paths. This study employs geometric TDI paired with a ternary search to investigate combinations of modified second-generation TDI solutions. By analyzing how the rate of change in the opposite cyclic directions informs a comparison of arm-length variations, we distinguished between second-generation and modified second-generation approaches, ultimately utilizing fourteen-link configurations to identify nine distinct solutions within a recovered library originally.

Historically, quantum photodetection frameworks have divided into two approaches: one seeks to identify which quantum field observable corresponds to photoelectron detection, thereby providing the foundational logic for detection to occur; the other consists of phenomenological models that meticulously simulate the specific mechanics of individual detectors. This dissertation addresses the distinction within these established categories—the contemporary literature on photodetection—by developing a comprehensive quantum mechanical representation of the detection process, incorporating its three key stages: transmission, amplification, and subsequent classical measurement. This work is grounded in quantum information theory and employs the framework of positive operator valued measures (POVMs) for its formalization. Additionally, this dissertation synthesizes findings from three previously published papers: Propp & van Enk (2019) on improved quantum limits for photon counting via nonlinear amplification, Propp & van Enk (2019) detailing quantum architectures for single photon detection, and Propp & van Enk (2020) explaining methods for projecting arbitrary single-photon wavepackets.

Major online platforms such as Google supply numerous application program interfaces (APIs) that permit verified external services and applications to retrieve user account information, facilitating functions including single sign-on (SSO), calendar management, and bulk emailing, alongside other features. To investigate how Google users perceive third-party applications and their integration via API, the authors conducted two phases of an online survey.

In the initial phase, 432 respondents were asked to recall any third-party access granted; 82 percent indicated using at least one form of SSO, and roughly one half remembered authorizing at least one specific app. To gather deeper insight into specific authorizations and SSO practices, a second study recruited a fresh cohort of 214 users to detail their Google account integrations. Analysis revealed that 86 percent of Google users employed SSO, and nearly two-thirds maintained authorized third-party apps.

Following a detailed examination of these integrations, the research indicates a distinct disconnect between users':
*   **Primary fears:** Users exhibited significant anxiety concerning exposure of self-identity data, specifically email addresses and publicly viewable personal details.

The researchers speculate that the lower anxiety levels regarding invasive access might stem from trust transferance to Google, where apps appear to operate in a virtual partnership, leading users to assume these specific data accesses carry Google's inherent safety standards. Ultimately, the research outcomes offer pathways for optimizing Google's existing tools to manage third-party access. Recommendations include implementing tracking mechanisms to monitor recent app activity, enforcing automatic revocations based on prolonged inactivity, and refining permission control structures.

Marcus-Levich-Jortner (MLJ) theory remains one of the standard approaches for deriving electron-transfer rates and analyzing experimental data by accounting for nuclear quantum effects; it partitions a molecular problem where the subsystem is handled quantum-mechanically via Fermi's golden rule, while the solvent acts as a bath described by classical Marcus theory. Extending this concept, we introduce an enhanced "reduced" semiclassical instanton theory—a multiscale strategy that simulates quantum tunneling with molecular precision within an anharmonic subsystem subjected to a bath described by harmonic oscillators. We demonstrate that instanton theory offers substantially superior accuracy compared to both the semiclassical cumulant expansion and Franck-Condon sums, methods which can incur orders-of-magnitude inaccuracies and typically neglect the principle of detailed balance. Unlike wavefunction-dependent MLJ theory, instanton methodology relies on path integrals; consequently, it bypasses the need to solve the Schr¨odinger equation or require full prior knowledge of the subsystem's potential energy surfaces for all relevant states. This allows it to handle intricate, anharmonic, multidimensional subsystems effectively with no additional approximating assumptions. Beyond yielding highly accurate reaction probabilities, instanton theory elucidates the reaction mechanism by identifying the principal tunneling trajectory and characterizing the vibrational states of reactant and product species interacting within an environmental bath akin to results derived from MLJ theory.

Although employing counting methodologies to address unambiguity in standard finite alphabet structures has long been established in classic literature, its extension to infinite alphabets and register automata represents a new approach for this work. The Shapley value has emerged as a prevalent tool for explaining predictions from varying degrees of machine learning models, from simple to complex systems. Our paper investigates the factors driving variations in Shapley values. A central question is whether the feature distribution correlates with the magnitude of its Shapley value. Furthermore, we analyze how Shapley explanations differ even for outcomes derived from identical models, such as transitioning between probabilities log‑odds and discrete classifications within a single logistic or probit framework. Our findings suggest that a feature's Shapley value depends on multiple statistical moments—particularly variance in addition to the mean—creating significant inconsistencies not only regarding baseline choices but also concerning feature sign and the ranking of most influential variables across different output types. Quantum devices surpass classical ones in application but require error-rate verification below specific thresholds to function correctly. Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) has recently gained considerable attention for enhancing non-line-of-sight radar remote sensing. Previous research predominantly concentrated on designing single IRS beamformers for this specific application. However, this study, for the first time in the literature, examines an multi-IRS-aided multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar framework, jointly optimizing unimodular transmit waveforms and optimal IRS beamformers. Utilizing the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) of target direction-of-arrival (DoA) as a performance metric, we acknowledge that hardware constraints favor unimodular transmission sequences. By employing suitable transformations, we reformulate the joint design challenge into two unimodular quadratic programming (UQP) problems. Given the NP-hard characteristics of these problems, we introduce the UBeR (unimodular waveform and beamforming design) algorithm for multi-IRS radar, which leverages computationally efficient, power-method-inspired iterations. Numerical results demonstrate that DoA estimation CRLBs are notably improved when utilizing the resulting MIMO waveforms and phase shifts generated by our UBeR approach.

Furthermore, we compared the performance of these detected signals when generated using a one-stage versus our proposed two-stage configuration.

Quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (QKSD) offers a cost-effective alternative to standard quantum phase estimation for calculating the ground and excited state energies of many-body quantum systems. However, typical QKSD methods rely on the Hadamard test for matrix elements of $\langle \phi_i|e^{-i\hat{H}\tau}|\phi_j \rangle$, demanding ancilla qubits and controlled multi-qubit gates that are expensive for near-term devices. This paper argues that a broad category of Hamiltonians central to quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics possesses symmetries that bypass the need for the Hadamard test entirely. We introduce a multi-fidelity protocol capable of evaluating these terms; when paired with efficient single-fidelity methods, it significantly cuts down circuit depth. Furthermore, this work establishes a unified theoretical framework for Quantum Krylov algorithms and details three novel quantum-classical approaches for estimating energies, each offering distinct trade-offs in terms of total quantum calls, circuit gate depth, computational complexity for the classical component, and stability regarding the generalized eigenvalue problem.

Graphene plasmons have garnered considerable interest owing to their adjustability, potential for extended propagation, and ultra-short wavelengths; however, the latter feature complicates light-plasmon interaction, typically necessitating elaborate coupling arrangements, extremely high doping, and graphene nanostructuring that challenge the limits of present lithography. To address this technical difficulty, the present work introduces a theoretically demonstrated approach utilizing a specific substrate: one with low and negative dielectric properties that intrinsically extends the graphene polariton wavelength to manageable scales. We focus on silicon carbide (SiC), which, within the mid-infrared spectral window (951–970 cm$^{-1}$), exhibits real and imaginary parts in its dielectric function between -1,0 and < 0.05. Computational analysis reveals hybridization with the substrate's phonon polariton, yieldig a polariton wavelength ten times greater—and correspondantly enhancing propagation by the same ratio—compared to the outcomes observed with a silicon dioxide reference substrate.

On a 7-manifold, one can construct two unique Einstein metrics: the 3-Sasakian metric and the squashing-induced Einstein metric. Since the 3-Sasakian structure also yields nearly parallel $G_2$-structures that generate these metrics, these geometric structures are central to the definition of both Einstein metrics. In analogy with how the Ricci flow (up to scaling) stabilizes at Einstein metrics, nearly parallel $G_2$-structures act as natural stationary solutions (up to scaling) within the geometric frameworks of the Laplacian and coflow flows acting onto all $G_2$-structures. We specifically analyze these flows in environments exhibiting 3-Sasakian symmetry; while their dynamics offer parallels, their methods yield notably disconnected behaviors mainly concerning the stability aspects of the nearly parallel $G_2$-structures. We integrate our findings into a broader discussion comparing the behavior of the Laplacian flows with the (rescaled) Ricci flow.

Virtual Try-On (VTON) enhances e-retailing by enabling customers to try on clothes from the comfort of their homes; however, existing VTON methods often struggle to generate consistent results for users posed with bent arms. This issue is particularly pronounced for long sleeves due to the risk of conflicting overlaps between clothing parts in such postures. Current warping techniques relying on Thin Plate Spline (TPS) transformations fail to address this problem effectively. Consequently, this work proposes a solution by segmenting source clothing into logical parts, each warped independently to fit the target body shape to better accommodate bent arm postures utilizing hand-crafted, geometry-consistent features. Additionally, the study introduces two learned components: a synthesis network and a mask prediction module. These elements combined yield a photo-realistic and pose-robust VTON approach without necessitating paired training datasets, while comparative analysis against existing benchmarks demonstrates method robustness.

Chest X-Ray (CXR) imagery is a primary tool for clinical screening and diagnosis. Automating the creation of radiologist reports on these images could significantly ease the burden on radiologic technologists who otherwise spend considerable time describing results and forming conclusions. However, the intricate structures linking and existing within report sections present a significant hurdle to automatic generation. Specifically, an 'Impression' acts as a diagnostic synthesis of the 'Findings' section, yet the prevalence of normal findings often outweighs abnormal ones. Existing research largely ignores this core structural hierarchy and data imbalance. Addressing this, we propose a new framework that utilizes inter- and intra-sectional report structures to generate XR reports: initially employing a two-phase strategy that explicitly maps 'Impressions' back to 'Findings' within a cooperative multi-agent system, and subsequently design a mechanism that subtly manages the skewed balance between abnormal and normal data to capture this dependency. Testing across two CXR report datasets demonstrates superior results using various metrics compared to current methods, proving that incorporating these structural elements produces high-quality medical reporting.

This reliance on OLS necessitates extensive data durations for validity and leaves the method vulnerable to confounding variables. This work addresses by proposing and applying LASSO-based statistics under sparse linear autoregressive assumptions, thereby investigating strong finite-sample (non-asymptotic) behavior. Our analysis proves that the sparse identification conditions used in LASSO also enable the robust detection of Granger causality in models, while we analyze the false alarm rate inherent in simple thresholding rules for causal effects. Additionally, simulation and real-world datasets are utilized here; comparing LASSO performance against standard least-squares methods in causal discovery offers evidence supporting our theoretical findings and showcases robust detection capabilities even with short sample periods where OLS often under-delivers.

We introduce a framework for the complete, end-to-end optimization of metasurface imaging systems that employ compressed sensing to reconstruct targets based on their sparsity—meaning the object contains a small number of significant non-zero values at unknown locations. Our approach nests an iterative, unapproximated compressed sensing reconstruction process into an optimization pipeline, creating a data-efficient and interpretable method that maximizes the use of metaoptics in this manner. This methodology was applied to high-resolution phase-change material applications, including depth and imaging super-resolution, where the end-to-end design autonomously determines optimal physical parameters for metasurfaces tailored to sparsity recovery. This process seamlessly navigates intricate theoretical tradeoffs and complex constraints involved. Furthermore, these optimized systems proved highly robust to noise; outperforming random scattering surfaces and closely approaching the theoretical limits achievable by ideal Gaussian random matrices in compressed sensing applications. Overall, these results establish that physical dynamic systems can achieve performance nearly matching the best mathematical benchmarks for compressed sampling techniques.

Ensuring the privacy of machine learning algorithms remains a critical bottleneck for the widespread deployment of Artificial Intelligence. Addressing this specifically within image datasets featuring facial representations, our work highlights the growing necessity of anonymization, driven by the extensive data collection from surveillance systems used for autonomous vehicles, among other applications. While existing approaches primarily obscure identities by altering pixel-space attributes, our study instead projects these images into a latent space using Generation Against Networks (GANs). The proposed method identifies features offering maximal identity disentanglement to preserve distinguishing visual traits and then manipulates these features across the image dataset, the GAN latent space, or through modification in both domains simultaneously or in conjunction with pixel transformations. A key outcome of the work is the development of the StyleID framework, designed to facilitate feature preservation while ensuring robust anonymization and individual privacy, and maximizing retention of the underlying characteristics within image datasets. The research introduces a novel measure and complementary methods to evaluate disentanglement alongside fresh theoretical contributions to identity dissociation. Furthermore, StyleID offers configurable levels of anonymity and maintains high computational efficiency, outperforming the state-of-the-art anonymizers.

This study proposes a flexible and selectable resource framework to alleviate both voltage and congestion thermal issues within distribution networks (DNs). The core of the methodology involves computing flexibility activation signals (FAS), where calculation is driven by the current state of the DN excluding these potential flexible resources. The signal design draws inspiration from inverters with volt-Var and volt-Watt control schemes, shares characteristics with local marginal prices (optimal power flow duals), and operates proactively via an inverse-response or drooping mechanism to prevent violations rather than correcting them post-occurrence. The research addresses nonlinear resource dispatch via second-order cone (SOC) relaxation to enable optimal flow analysis through convexification. Subsequently, three specific case studies, evaluated with proprietary performance metrics, demonstrate the framework's capabilities. The first case illustrates the multi-objective dynamics of the relaxed RDOPF and offers Pareto tuning strategies that minimize both DN energy losses and the optimality gap of the relaxation method relative to nonlinear models. The second study outlines a strategy for Distribution System Operators to plan for temporally and location-specific flexibility requirements in the DN. The final case quantifies the effect of reactive power flexibility across different load power factor scenarios, finding that active power flexibility requirements can diminish by as much as half when the power factor is set to 0.8.

The rising integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) causes continuously evolving operating scenarios that distribution grid operators must handle efficiently. The intermittency associated with renewable sources, such as solar photovoltaics, alongside load forecasting inaccuracies, heighten grid uncertainty and introduce major power quality issues like voltage magnitude breaches and unbalance. To mitigate the impact of this variability on grid operations, this study employs an optimization method based on constraints handling chance probabilities. We introduce and formulate the three-phase distribution chance-constrained optimal power flow (CC-OPF) problem; through this process, the work addresses a revised model utilizing constraint tightening that eliminates the need for relaxing or approximating the three-phase AC power flow equations. Subsequently, the authors develop two iterative algorithms designed to solve this reformulation efficiently. Just-in-time (JIT) compilation and code caching generally speed up dynamic language execution, yet both the cache memory for hot code and the resource-intensive profiling required consume considerable RAM. Consequently, generating this cached information adds significant compilation latency. Current Android environments typically isolate JIT compilers and code caches per process, preventing sharing among distinct applications on the similar devices. However, because these apps often utilize shared public libraries across multiple processes or even applications simultaneously, pooling cached bytecode could reduce RAM usage and compilation duration while simultaneously cutting back interpretation time; all three factors ultimately enhance runtime speed.

This paper presents ShareJIT: a system implementing global memory that enables JIT compilers to share compiled objects across diverse applications and processes using the currently dominant version, the ART for Android. To maximize sharing potential over traditional compilation, the system limits JIT contextual optimization, thereby highlighting the core trade-off of reducing stack-adaptability to enhance global shareability. Experiments conducted ShareJIT across 30 runs involving eight leading Android applications yielded a 9% gain in average performance, decreased memory consumption by 16%, and reduced JIT compilation time by 37%.

Creating automated systems that produce genuinely creative text has long been an aspiration. Recent scholarly interest has shifted focus toward leveraging these technologies to boost human writers' capacity for creative expression. This study centers on how humans are influenced by witnessing automatically generated outputs. specifically, we investigate the task of sentence infilling—convincing a given list into words into full narratives. We define a favorable quality in these sentences as "storability," meaning the text hints at a narrative that piques reader curiosity.

We compared human performance against an automated system utilizing a neural language model on this sentence infilling challenge. Under two different conditions, participants were asked to compose these sentences: one condition without external aid, and the other where they viewed model-generated sentences alongside their own composition tasks. The participants were then asked to rate each sentence for its storability.

Our findings indicate two key outcomes: first, sentences crafted by humans were evaluated as more interesting when participants had seen the model's examples beforehand; second, the perceived "storability" grew with increasing semantic influence drawn from those observed examples. These results suggest a paradigm termed"Inspiration Through Observation"within human-computer co-creation. This approach demonstrates that text generation models can enrich human writing by providing creative inspiration rather than immediate copywriting solutions.

We demonstrate that the controlled time evolution technique, where a system evolves conditionally on an ancilla qubit's state, can be efficiently implemented via controlled reversal gates. A reversal gate $R$ consists of single-qubit operations that anticommute with a specific subset of Hamiltonian terms, and its controlled variant $C_R$ applies $R$ only if the ancilla qubit holds a defined state. Through sign inversion of Hamiltonian terms linked to the ancilla's conditionality, the temporal evolution is effectively toggled between forward and backward directions. Leveraging this method alongside the rod and algorithm to analyze the energy spectrum of a two-qubit Hamiltonian, we show that employing controlled reversal gates can decrease the count of required two-qubit entangling gates by a factor of five. Experiments utilizing Quantinuum H1-2 and IBM Perth hardware successfully determined the corresponding energy levels; although the Quantinuum device exhibited a significantly lower error rate, both setups achieved spectral determination with an error margin below 0.06% of the spectrum's total span using five algorithm cycles of the rod and algorithm implementation. Furthermore, an analysis of projected scalability suggests that the gate-count reduction becomes even more pronounced for larger, many-body quantum systems.

Electric dipole moment measurements offer a sensitive method for detecting new phases within the Higgs Yukawa interactions. This paper examines the creation of harmonics in graphene subjected to an artificial magnetic field produced by mechanical deformation of a graphene flake. Our findings illustrate that the Landau level structure induced by this pseudomagnetic field disrupts the material's centrosymmetry, enabling the production of even harmonics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that depending on the duration of the impinging pulse, the resulting nonlinear signal comprises not only integer multiples of the driving pulse frequency but also half-integer harmonics, a characteristic resulting from the unique square-root dependence of graphene's Landau energy levels.

This study examines a type-II extended complex singlet scalar model with $Z_3$ symmetry capable of simultaneously addressing dark matter abundance, non-vivial neutrino masses, and cosmic baryon asymmetry, wherein the complex singlet scalar constitutes the dark matter candidate. By analyzing the thermal evolution, we map specific parameter regions enabling a strongly first-order electroweak phase transition (SFOEWPT) in the early universe; the stochastic gravitational wave signatures from such an event may become detectable using next-generation space and land-based observatories. We specifically investigate how the interplay between the quartet and invisible scalar sectors reshapes the Higgs potential to favor the SFOEWPT. While light mass states within the triplet sector naturally support such a transition, we restrict our analysis to regions satisfying LHC constraints on such states. Conversely, although no heavier states were required under natural lightness, recent LHC precision Higgs measurements via di-leptonic decays effectively exclude most viable regions capable of inducing the transition. Additionally, stringent spin-independent direct detection results from collaborations such as XENON-10T or PANDA-4C eliminate significant viable regions associated with dark sector modifications to the SM Higgs potential unless dark matter is significantly undense. We conclude that the non-observation of new physics in future LHC or direct DM detection campaigns will severely compromise the prospects for GW detection and rule out the mechanisms of electroweak baryogenesis within this framework.

Deep neural architectures can handle numerous tasks when abundant labeled data exists; indeed, limited labeled data represents the primary constraint, particularly in settings like semi-supervised learning that suffer from data scarcity. Human assessments further verified the quality of distilled evidence. Results demonstrate that automatically generated evidential data effectively replicates human levels of clarity, brevity, informativism, ultimately serving to enhance the interpretability of provided solutions.

This work introduces a new data-centric method for developing machine learning algorithms capable of effective performance with minimal labeled data. Furthermore, we present a strategy for integrating disparate similarity metrics and optimizing multiple hyperparameters, offering versatile tools for broad problem classes. The methodologies derived hold potential value extending beyond semi-supervised learning to data-driven solutions for combinatorial challenges.

Implementing Bayesian inference on complex hierarchical structures is riddled with computational challenges. While sampling-based methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo are celebrated for their accuracy, they suffer from high resource demands and often experience sluggish or unreliable convergence. By contrast, Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), an approximate technique, constructs univariate posterior determinisms through nested Laplace procedures, offering rapid inference specifically tailored to the Latent Gaussian Models encompassing many hierarchical structures. Of the primary inference strategies used in the R-INLA software suite to generate required posterior estimates based on precision needs, Simplified Laplace Approximation (SLA) was historically preferred for its speed, given its reliance on the third-order Taylor expansion of full Laplace approximations. We refine this methodology by streamlining calculations related to skew and posterior mass configurations, subsequently proposing a fourth-order expansion utilizing the Extended Skew Normal distribution as the fitting mechanism. Empirical results suggest that our improved marginal posterior density approximations outperformed SLA in accuracy without imposing any significant additional computational expense.

Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) is increasingly utilized across various domains but traditionally requires repeatedly solving constrained nonlinear optimization problems in real-time, online settings using an iterative numerical procedure that is computationally demanding and error-prone to local optima. This research examines the relationship between Monte Carlo sampling techniques and Bayesian estimation within the framework of NMPC. We introduce and explore a constraint-aware particle smooth­ing/filtering protocol capable of efficiently and straightforwardly operationalizing sampling-based NMPC, especially for complex nonlinear cases where traditional optimization strategies find handling high dimensions challenging and error-prone to local optima. We test and assess the effectiveness of our new algorithm via simulation. We demonstrate how the sampling method offers computational advantages to traditional approaches like the Monte Carlo particle filters. We examine NMPC algorithms using a particle smooth filter or smoothing approach while maintaining certain safety boundaries. The proposed work targets efficiency and scalability alongside computational complexity reduction that may help mitigate issues faced by standard nonlinear methods through numerical optimization procedures which can become trapped in poor solutions. We demonstrate the robustness using a case study.

During the emergence of highly infectious diseases with superior transmission and mortality risks, access to vaccines and drugs is typically scarce. However, a critical reality involves an additional transmission pathway: anonymous, unpredictable exposures where tracing fixed contacts proves ineffective. This study models such realistic scenarios using a susceptible-infected-recovered framework applied to multiplex networks with isolation protocols. These networks consist of two layers—a fixed interaction layer and a layer featuring random, time-dependent contacts—to simulate different spread mechanisms. By treating the fixed contacts as quenched disorder and random interactions as annealed disorder, the research proposes a strategic preemptive isolation protocol. This approach involves isolating not only direct but also second-level neighbors of infected hospital patients, comparing this method to those widely utilized globally. Numerical simulations indicate that this proactive measure significantly reduces both the total epidemic size and the number of isolates required per unit of time. These results highlight a more effective strategy for managing various disease outbreaks, even when full contact tracing capabilities are unavailable.

Although many toolkits have been created to facilitate the ethical development of artificial intelligence, every tool inherently encodes design choices and presuppositions regarding how work ought to be performed and executed. This paper presents a qualitative analysis of 27 AI ethics toolkits to critically explore how they conceptualize ethical efforts and provide support for them. The study investigates the narratives these toolkits utilize when discussing ethical issues, their assumptions about which actors bear responsibility for this work, and how they model workplace practices for resolving ethics concerns. Our findings suggest that AI ethics toolkits primarily cast such ethical work as a technical pursuit suitable for solitary technologists, even as advocates push for broader stakeholder involvement in addressing AI's social complexities. Moreover, these tools often fail to engage with the organizational or political dimensions of implementing ethics in practice. Consistently, we observe a disconnect between how the toolkits conceptualize ethical duties and how they actually enable the execution of those duties. notably, there is a conspicuous absence of direction on navigating the organizational power dynamics essential to performing ethical interventions. Consequently, we highlight these gaps to offer a framework for advancing the research and development of effective AI ethics toolkits by future scholars and practitioners.

This study addresses the challenges of controlling and modeling robot teams tasked with long-term environmental data collection across specific areas. While traditional low-level, reactive assignments struggle to scale with increased numbers of units and locations due to costly replanning needs, conventional top-level approaches often only account for transit times rather than comprehensive task dynamics. This work examines a specific class of nonlinear macroscopic models to regulate time-evolving robot distributions as they execute various activities. Our suggested ensemble modeling framework controls the population distribution by utilizing the organic social interactions at play. Validated through experimental multi-fidelity results, including physical trials, this method demonstrates effectiveness in executing robust environmental monitoring operations.

Users relying on artificial intelligence decision-aids frequently exhibit excessive trust, accepting incorrect recommendations prompted by the system. Introducing explanations to clarify AI judgments fails to mitigate this tendency; in some cases, it appears to exacerbate it. Guided by the dual-process cognitive framework, we propose that individuals rarely scrutinize each AI suggestion or explanation deeply. Instead, they tend to rely on heuristics regarding when to trust the system based on past interactions. Extanding on previous research into healthcare decision-making, we developed three "cognitive forcing" interventions designed to compel a more reflective engagement with AI explanations. In an experiment involving 199 participants, we evaluated our three intervention designs against standard explainable AI baselines and a control group using the AI independently (no intervention). Results indicate that while cognitive forcing effectively diminished overreliance compared to basic explanatory AI, it presented a significant trade-off: users provided the lowest ratings to these high-proximity strategies. Furthermore, an audit for intervention-induced bias revealed that participants with a higher motivation to engage efforts (referred as "High Need for Cognition") gained the most from these methods on average; conversely, others benefit less noticeably. Consequently, our research underscores how an individual's intrinsic cognitive drive can modulate or limit the efficacy of explainable AI implementations.

Investigating alterations in brain functional connectivity for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) necessitates the analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data. Predicting the condition of vegetation in reaction to meteorological conditions and climatic occurrences constitutes a significant hurdle. Successfully executing this task is vital for forecasting agricultural output, ecological damage to forests, or broader alterations in services provided by ecosystems that support socio-economic stability; a prediction failure could trigger humanitarian catastrophes. The physiological state of vegetation is determined by specific weather and environmental factors that regulate complex ecological mechanisms operating across numerous time scales. The interplay between flora and various environmental drivers generates both immediate and time-delayed responses, frequently revealing spatial patterns at regional and landscape magnitudes. We define the land surface forecasting problem akin to strongly guided video prediction, aimed at anticipating vegetation development with high granularity by directing the model using weather and topographic variables. Employing a Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) architecture, the proposed system forecasts shifts in vegetation metrics across Africa using Sentinel-derived 2 NDVI as the primary indicator, while integrating ERA5 atmospheric data, satellite soil moisture readings from SMAP, and SRTM digital terrain modes as guiding features. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that ConvLSTM frameworks possess the capacity to predict high-resolution seasonal trends in vegetation indices alongside diverse effects of meteorological deviations from baseline levels. Notably, the model distinguishes between varying forest types, even when exhibiting substantial variability over time, an attribute deemed promising for facilitating pre-emptive interventions regarding drought-induced calamities.

Live blogging has emerged as a prominent method in online journalism for delivering real-time coverage of breaking stories and occurring events worldwide, providing minute-by-minute reader updates. Furthermore, to support the broader academic community in reproducing findings and continuing research, the author suite of tools for corpus reconstruction are made openly available to the public.

Disordered rocksalt Li3V2O5 offers a promising solution as the anode for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, distinguished by its ideal low-voltage potential, high-rate performance, and excellent cycling durability. This study presents an extensive investigation into the intercalation mechanisms of DRX-Li3V2O5 anodes by combining density functional theory with machine learning cluster expansions and interatomic potentials. The voltage profile predicted for room-temperature DRX-Li3V2O5 using a calibrated cluster expansion model alongside Monte Carlo simulations aligns closely with experimental observations. Contrasting earlier density functional theory outcomes, our results indicate that during charging, Li ions primarily intercalate into tetrahedral sites with a significant majority of Li and V atoms retaining stability upon octahedral sites. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations employing a calibrated moment tensor potential identify the system's fast-charging capability to stem from the efficient Li+ diffusivity along the specific tetrahedral-octahedral-tetrahedral pathway. The study also recommends adjusting the Li:V ratio to balance enhanced lithiation capacity against necessary anodic voltage trade-offs for this specific configuration. Ultimately, this research delivers detailed mechanistic insights into high-performance DRX-Li3V2O5 anodes, facilitating future discoveries of novel disordered materials.

Classifying music genre based solely on lyrics represents one of the most difficult problems within Music Information Retrieval. This study utilizes recurrent neural networks on an extensive corpus of complete song lyrics. Evaluations conducted on both comprehensive 118-genre and condensed 20-genre datasets demonstrated that HAN surpasses both non-neural approaches and simpler neural alternatives, outperforming prior research by covering a broad spectrum of genres. During this training, the system's ability to identify which specific lines or lyrics deemed most influential for genre classification was rendered through visualization. Consequently, HAN elucidates the computational aspects of lyrical architecture and linguistic markers that effectively distinguish various musical categories.

As an output, a Vis2Mus system acts as a controllable user experience tool that generates musical expression patterns from visual stimuli.

How can RL agents in a shared setting autonomously acquire diverse cooperative behaviors? While single-agent models successfully combine goal-conditioned policies with intrinsic motivation to master various independently discovered objectives, applying this to Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems (CIS) presents difficulties: agents sampling goals independently struggle to converge on unified cooperative goals, thus hindering learning efficacy. Addressing this, we propose the Decentralized Intrinsically Motivated Skill Acquisition Problem (Dec-IMSAP) to model and solve cooperative navigation scenarios. Unlike prior works that rely on centralized goal-selection, Dec-IRS agents train fully in a decentralized manner. Empirical results demonstrate that efficient acquisition of diverse cooperative tasks requires goal alignment, where agents pursue identical shared objectives while coordinating actions through specialized roles. Furthermore, we present the Goal-coordination game, a framework for fully-decentralized, emergent communications wherein goal synchronization naturally emerges from individual reward maximization within multi-goal settings. This approach matches the performance of centralized baselines with guaranteed goal alignment and represents, to our knowledge, the first investigation into intra-momentary multi-agent exploration of goals under fully-decentralized training conditions.
