Most extant extractive summarization techniques operate by selecting $N$ of the most crucial sentences from a text to form the summary, yet few studies investigate the extraction of finer-grained Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs), nor have they comprehensively analyzed or validated these unit selections. This paper fills that void through initial explorative research and analysis, which not merely compares the performance ceiling of sentence-based approaches against EDU-centric methods but also demonstrates from a conceptual and experimental perspective that employing EDUs yields more concise and precise summaries without discarding salient information. Leveraging this advantage, the authors introduce an innovative EDU-level summarize model named Variable-Length EDU (VL) Summarizing (VL), which incorporates specific learning algorithms designed for EDU-level text analysis and creation. The developed model is refined to encode information within an independent text corpus with varying degrees of dependency, identify candidate summaries of different lengths, and optimize summary selection. The methods are applied to multiple benchmarks of single or multi-level domains, showcasing enhanced results compared to existing best-performing algorithms without loss of summarization quality.

The strong robustness of trained neural networks against significant pruning, alongside the increasing scale of modern architecture, has driven substantial investigation into sparse modeling. This study specifically addresses the challenge of regulating sparsity levels during sparse learning. Current techniques that rely on penalties require costly, trial-and-error adjustments to their hyperparameters, preventing direct specification of sparsity. To address this limitation, we implement a constrained approach that integrates the Gate mechanism introduced by Louizos et al. (2018). This method frames the process as an optimization problem where model sparsification is steered both by the learning task and specific sparsity goals in an integrated, end-to-end manner. Empirical results on WideResNet and ResNet architectures using datasets from CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet confirm the method's success, demonstrating a novel capability to meet predetermined sparsity thresholds without degrading predictive accuracy.

Large convolutional neural networks often suffer from significant generalization gaps when trained on scarce labeled datasets; to counter this, emerging methods mix pairs of examples to create synthetic training samples. This paper proposes PatchUp, a regularization method operating at the block-level of hidden states within CNNs. It applies to contiguous segments of feature map blocks generated randomly from two instances. Our approach strengthens CNN resilience against manifold intrusion, a risk present in current state-of-the-art mixing strategies like Mixup and CutMix. Furthermore, by blending high-dimensional continuous feature blocks within the latent space rather than lower-dimensional input pixels, PocketUp yields a training set of samples that is exceptionally diverse across different dimensions. Experiments conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN using architectures such as PreactResNet-18, PlectResNet-34, and WideResNet-28-10 demonstrate that PatchUp achieves performance at least comparable to or superior to modern regularizers. Additionally, our results confirm that it enhances generalization under affine image transformations and offers greater resistance to adversarial attacks.

While specific strongly correlated material classes offer significant promise for high thermopower efficiency, a complete comprehension of how electronic correlations influence the Seebeck coefficient remains elusive. This gap stems in part from the boundary conditions of standard Boltzmann frameworks. Consequently, there exists an urgency to establish a thermopower formula capable of distinguishing between kinetic and potential energy roles in the variations observed during changes in temperature and carrier doping. This study resolves that requirement by formulating, for lattices exhibiting Hubbard-type interactions, an expression isolating these energy sources; moreover, this derivation may refine the comprehension surrounding correlation-driven modifications of thermal voltage. To illustrate the framework, thermopower evaluations for the one-band Hubbard model are conducted utilizing dynamical mean-field theory. Results demonstrate that within the realm of both intermediate and strong correlations, impacts derived from kinetic and potential energies almost completely offset one another.

We describe techniques for (i) visually identifying reliable (sub)millimeter spectroscopic redshifts through emission lines, (ii) assessing how effectively various (sub)mm methods determine spectroscopic redshifts, and (iii) enhancing future observation strategies to raise the proportion of secure redshift measurements. Leveraging publicly accessible code (https://github.com/tjlcbakx/redshift-search-graphs), we examine cases where robust redshifts emerge from both single-line and multi-line detections, as well as instances where ambiguity persists despite multiple detections. Drawing on redshift distributions derived from existing samples, we evaluate the efficiency of diverse redshift-measurement techniques, covering interferometers alongside instruments tailored for redshift discovery from current and future facilities. Concluding our analysis offers a methodology for refining observation protocols for upcoming Atacama Large Millimetre/submillimetre Array redshift projects, highlighting the essential role of 2 mm observations in securing robust measurements within the z = 2 – 4 range.

For a fashion outfit to be visually pleasing, its constituent garments must align visually in style, category, and color. Addressing this limitation, we introduce Visual Incompatibility TRANSfOrmer (VICTOR), which is designed to perform overall compatibility as a continuous range assessment alongside the identification of mismatching items by leveraging clothing-aware contrastive language-image pre-training. We expand the existing Polyvore benchmark through curated partial mismatches, creating a novel training set called Polyvore-MISFITs. Comprehensive experimentation demonstrates that this architecture rivals, and occasionally exceeds, the performance of state-of-the-art methods on Polyvore benchmarks while cutting per-instance floating-point operations by 88%, thus achieving an optimal balance of speed and efficacy. The word embedding association test (WEAT) is a critical tool for assessing language bias toward social groups like racial minorities within extensive text collections by evaluating the semantic proximity between group-representative entities (e.g., distinct names) and descriptive attribute words (e.g., "pleasant" vs. "unpleasant"). Analysis reveals that anti-black WEAT scores derived from geo-tagged social media posts at the metropolitan statistical area level align closely with multiple indicators of racial bias. Crucially, however, these alignments persist even when adjusting for various sociodemographic factors, yet every significant correlation is fully accounted for by a third variable: the relative frequency of Black versus White names in the data. The expansion of open access (OA) has heightened the intricacy of financial dynamics within scholarly journal publishing, even as comprehensive data and clarity regarding these transactions remain scarce. Results demonstrate that our solution successfully identifies attacks with high precision while imposing minimal computational cost on server operations.

This study addresses social link inference within a target Location-aware Social Network (LSN), focusing on the task of predicting unconnected relationships between users. Such predictions are pivotal for downstream tasks like network completion and friend recommendations. While general link prediction often relies on network structure, recent efforts addressing social link inference in LSIs also integrate user trajectories spatially; however, the temporal dimensions within these trajectories are frequently neglected, hindering the model's ability to capture time-based relevance. Consequently, the effective synthesis of multiple perspectives—social, spatial, and temporal—to match users remains an open challenge impeding further improvements in link inference. To address this, we propose a novel Multi-View Matching Network (MVMN) that treats social, spatial, and temporal factors as distinct views of a target user pair. MVMN flexibly leverages custom matching modules to model these factors: a location matching module, a time-series matching module, and a relation matching module. These modules jointly learn view-specific representations, which MVMN subsequently fuses for precise link inference. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets confirm that our approach outperforms competitive baselines in link prediction and sequence matching, highlighting the value of its core components.

This paper introduces a joint synthesis approach designed for trajectory and a controlled invariant funnel (CIF) to be effective for locally Lipschitz nonlinear systems facing bounded external disturbances. The proposed recursive scheme focuses on enhancing two main elements: (1) updating the trajectory and (2) updating the funnel. As an end product, any path derived from the starting point and evolved using the designed control law stays within a secure region relative to the trajectory when bounded disturbances are present, including the consideration for obstacle avoidance in 3D path planning.

Given the unreliability of human Internet workers, fulfilling crowdsourcing objectives satisfactorily is challenging, particularly within multiple tasks where financial constraints exist. Recently, meta-learning has revitalized few-shot learning, enabling classifiers to deliver fair performance with minimal training data. This study introduces the \textquotedbl{}meta-worker,' a machine annotator employed in types of tasks (such as image classification) well-suited for artificial intelligence that are difficult for humans. Unlike standard crowdworkers, meta-workers are reliable, consistent, tireless, and free. Our method clusters unlabeled data and requests human annotators to label instances surrounding the center of those clusters. Using this annotated data alongside meta-training datasets, various meta-learning algorithms generate diverse meta-workers which subsequently handle the remaining crowdsourcing tasks. Disagreements between meta-workers' annotations are gauged using Jensen-Shannon entropy; if variance exists, this signals a need for human workers to refine the annotation further. Finally, meta-workers' specific preferences are modeled to calculate consensus outcomes via weighted majority voting. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that integrating human intelligence with computational capabilities via this framework can complete crowdsourcing projects at a lower budget cost than current optimal task allocation approaches while maintaining superior quality.

Guaranteeing the quality of automated driving systems represents a significant hurdle for the automotive sector. In this field, "quality" refers to the degree to which a system fulfills its specific expectations and specifications; notably, vehicles at SAE Level 4 and 5 must execute complex scenarios safely across diverse environments without failure, necessitating a systematic methodology to validate their safety. Since comprehensive real-world testing is unworkable, simulation-based testing offers the primary solution, wherein data used to assess driving system performance is generated digitally. For these simulations to be reliable indicators of quality, they themselves—encompassing models and architecture—must meet rigorous standards determined by their intended use. To address various testing contexts, it is essential to distinguish among three quality dimensions: that of the automated driving system and that of the simulation environment, which further divides into the quality of its component and background scenarios. Consequently, evaluating and verifying quality must become an integral part of every stage in system development and simulation. We propose a structured taxonomy in this study aimed at clarifying quality concepts within these processes, establishing clear boundaries to direct further testing efforts across the driven system and the comprehensive simulation, including its constituent models and test scenarios.

In telecommunications and radar applications, constructing Doppler-resilient sequences (DRSs) that maintain low sidelobe levels throughout the full range of signal delays and bandwidth shifts presents a challenging endeavor. However, since operational Doppler frequencies are typically much lower than signal bandwidths—and perfect synchronization is more feasible for short-duration delays than for the full signal window—we propose a focused approach using the Low Ambiguity Zone (LAZ). This specific region is defined within the signal's overall ambiguity function by targeted delay and frequency limits, consisting as the ideal "Zero Ambiguity Zone" (ZAZ) when the performance floor reaches zero across these parameters. Based on this premise, we derive theoretical limits for periodic DRSs possessing either fixed magnitudes, both with and without frequency domain restrictions, generalizing known bounds on the global periodic ambiguity function into particular instances. Furthermore, these limits serve to guide sequence design in evaluating their robustness against Doppler distortions. To meet those derived thresholds using fundamental algebraic techniques like additive number characters and cyclic difference sets on finite fields, we present four methods for constructing optimal DRSs specifically targeted for enhanced LAZ properties.

Optical frequency transfer enables highly accurate distribution of frequency over vast distances. A pivotal aspect of advancing technology in this field is its ability to convey high-spectral-purity signals derived from lasers stable on the ultrafine scale—or optical atomic clocks—to distant sites while simultaneously ensuring compatibility with established communication networks of diverse architectures. In this report, we introduce, to date, a novel method capable of distributing optical signals to multiple independent hubs along a circular optical fiber loop employing passive phase stabilization. The approach automatically compensates for fluctuations in optical path lengths at any number of nodes within the loop through signal mixing and frequency shifts. Functioning independently of active phase trackers or compensators, this methodology substantially alleviates specific technological obstacles inherent in traditional phase noise cancellation, namely restrictions in compensation speed, phase recovery delays, and phase jitter contamination arising from servo resonances ("bumps"). Furthermore, by utilizing bidirectional transmission via a single source, signal-to-noise ratio enhancements are realized at each hub. The method retains equivalent delay-bounded phase noise correction performance to established approaches while simultaneously tripling improvements in phase jitter. Consequently, this paves the way for the broad deployment of high-spectral-purity ultra-stable frequency references that exceed metroological applications, leveraging the inherent dependability and scalability of ring fiber networks.

A test scenario for an autonomous vehicle (AV) is deemed safety-critical whenever it uncovers a system malfunction. Because such events occur infrequently in standard traffic environments, simulations serve as the common tool for synthesizing them. AV driving scenarios are intricate, involving diverse dynamic and static features encompassed by other road users (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians), environmental factors like road surface and weather, and the AV itself. Due to this complexity, creating a comprehensive virtual test suite capable of identifying all critical scenarios proves impractical. This study introduces a systemic methodology utilizing Instance Space Analysis (ISA) to pinpoint specific features influencing a scenario's utility. ISA isolates the optimal set of features that distinguish critical failures from routine driving, visualizing how feature combinations relate to simulation results in an attempt. Visualization aids researchers to pinpoint regions of untested instance spaces where empirically possible yet currently uncovered test scenarios could yield valuable improvements—a key metric for assessing the quality. Additionally, we implemented four Machine Learning models trained to categorize scenarios as critical or not. High precision, recall, and F1-scores validate the effectiveness of this proposed framework, demonstrating that test scenario prioritizes efficiently by accurately forecasting the criticality of a scenario before execution.

Simulation-to-real learning, which involves training policies in simulated environments and transferring them for deployment on real hardware, represents a highly promising approach to data-efficient robotic learning. However, unavoidable discrepancies known as the "reality gap" often mean that a policy performing well in simulation can fail or behave unsafely in the real world. Consequently, direct adaptation on a robot carries the risks of self-damage or harm to the environment. To address this, we propose a novel learning framework called SafeAPT. This algorithm utilizes a diverse set of policies pre-evolved in simulation to identify and transfer a specific policy to the real robot through interactive episodes. SafeAPT accomplishes this by iteratively training both a safety model and a probabilistic reward model, leveraging a combination of real-time observations and simulated data as prior knowledge. Guided by these models, SafeAPT employs Bayesian optimization to select policies from the repertoire that maximize performance rewards while strictly adhering to safety constraints, thereby enabling safe robotic adaptation to various objectives without requiring new simulations. Experiments conducted in both simulated and real robotic settings demonstrate that compared to several baselines, SafeAPT is able to acquire high-performing policies within minutes on actual robots, significantly reducing the frequency and severity of violations during adaptation.

Our review rigorously examines the root of this divergence across both real space and multipole representations, identifying that it stems from the improper extrapolation of approximations beyond their limits of validity. Furthermore, while classical and quantum formulations share similar structures, their associated physical observables fundamentally differ. In contrast, the classical scenario expectantly yields a spatial overlap of transmitted and scattered waves to a wide extent downstream of the scatterer. As such, the calculated classical cross-section fails to directly represent a tangible physical observable in that regime.

Numerical plant models are capable of predicting the impact of performance outcomes resulting from trait changes induced by genetic variations, achieving this simulation by replicating physiological processes and their environmental interactions. Optimization techniques supplement these simulations to engineer ideotypes—defined as optimal trait combinations yielding the best adaptation to specific environmental and management conditions—usually by maximization of performance criteria like yield. As plant breeder reliance on simulation grows, numerical experiments must be rigorously constructed to yield precise, achievable outcomes grounded in biological accuracy. This study presents a multi-objective optimization framework combining a model-output performance metric with a feasibility metric that reflects observed trait corrrelations. When applied to two contrasting process-based and functional-plant models (sunflower and apple trees, respectively), this method effectively identified key plant traits and mapped solutions ranging from highly efficient to entirely realistic. This work validates the enhanced modeling strategy as capable of generating successful concepts while delivering clear guidance regarding trait modifications, specifying their direction and magnitude.

Recently, embedding-based knowledge graph (KG) models have enabled conjunctive querying over incomplete datasets, yet existing techniques primarily rely on inductive reasoning derived solely from data patterns. This approach fails to incorporate deducible reasoning using valuable external expertise such as ontology-based domain knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we enhance neural-symbolic ontology-mediated query processing within embedding spaces. Specifically, we implement distinct augmentation strategies to construct training samples via query rewriting and introduce a new loss function, resulting in a system that marginally surpasses baselines by effectively executing both the necessary inductive and deduction-based reasoning capabilities.

To resolve the numerical sign problem, we present a novel Hybrid Monte Carlo framework that utilizes molecular dynamics on continuum integration surfaces foliated by antiholomorphic gradient flow—defined as the integration surface's "worldvolume." Building upon the Tempered Lefschetz thimble (TLTM), this approach simultaneously addresses both the sign and multimodal challenges, mirroring the success of the original TLTM. Moreover, the generation of configurations in this new scheme bypasses the need to compute gradient flow Jacobians; such a computation is required solely to determine the relevant phase during final measurement steps. The efficacy of this algorithm is validated through its application to a chiral Random Matrix Model, a system where Complex Langevin dynamics are demonstrably incapable.

Imitation learning (IL) has become a leading strategy for tasks involving continuous control largely because it bypasses critical difficulties such as exploration challenges and reward misspecification commonly faced by reinforcement learning (RL). Within the framework of learning policies from demonstrations, ensuring these policies change smoothly in response to inputs remains a significant hurdle. This is especially problematic in large, complex state and action ($s$-$a$) spaces characteristic of high-dimensional continuous control scenarios. This work addresses this gap by integrating smoothness-inducing regularizers into both the policy and cost functions within models of adversarial imitation learning. These mechanisms enforce that the cost function transitions in a regulated fashion across the $s$-$a$ space while ensuring the resulting agent behavior is well-constrained by the state space. We designate this enhanced framework \textit{Smooth Policy and Cost Imitation Learning} (SPaCIL, pronounced 'Special'), introducing a novel metric to specifically evaluate policy smoothness. Experiments on contemporary MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that SPaCIL surpasses the state-of-the-art IL baseline on our specific smoothness measure while offering dual benefits: faster learning speeds and a significantly improved mean reward.

We address the challenge of synthesizing multi-action human motion sequences of indefinite duration. Our proposed iterative method produces smooth and realistic motions adaptable to any sequence length, maintaining linear complexity in both time and space. Trained and benchmarked on the PROX and Charades datasets—augmented respectively with ground-truth action labels and human poses—the model delivers state-of-the-art performance with superior FID scores and semantic alignment compared to existing approaches.

Identifying emotions within spoken speech often faces two main hurdles: effectively capturing speech features pertinent to emotions and accurately quantifying subjective, often noisy, emotional labels. By reducing classifier confidence in training labels through this approach, we achieved performance on the IEMOCAP dataset superior to existing literature. Recent scholarship has heavily focused on approximating and analyzing functions defined as expectations of a specific nonlinearity with regard to its stochastic internal weights, exemplified by "infinitely wide" networks using individual activation functions. We extend this theoretical framework to function representation via neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These neural SDEs are characterized as Itô diffusion processes where the drift term and diffusion matrix are drawn from specified parametric classes. We establish that determining whether a neural SDE can generate nonlinear mappings of its initial state corresponds to finding the optimal finite-time trajectory for steering an associated auxiliary dynamic system between designated endpoints. This auxiliary framework is formed deterministically by substituting standard Brownian motion with an explicit control variable within the original equation. Furthermore, we calculate theoretical bounds for the minimal control intensity requisite to achieve this trajectory, findings that possess standalone relevance for deterministic optimal control and motion planning applications.

To circumvent these limitations, we propose a new theoretical method for generating phonon angular momentum in the $\rm C_{60}$ molecular crystal. We demonstrate that a single laser pulse effectively injects substantial helicity-dependent angular momentum into the material, where the direction of rotation can be reversed by shifting from left- to right-circular polarization. On an ultrafast timescale, changes in orbital angular momentum mimic displacive coherent phonion excitations characterized by a time-dependent cosine waveform, distinct from spin dynamics. Crucially, despite strong laser driving, atomic displacements remain safely within the sub-Lindemann regime. Thermally induced rotation of $\rm C_{60}$ at room temperature alone yields massive angular momenta on the order of $\rm \sim10^1$-$\rm \sim10^5\hbar$ per molecule. This mechanism unlocks potential applications in a broader class of molecular solids, such as higher fullerenes ($\rm C_{n0}^{ }$) and their endohedral variants, enabling light- or heat-driven angular momentum generation. Such advancements facilitate strategies for opto-spin control of electronic systems and efficient harvesting of thermal energy via angular phononic modes.

In the initial phases of space mission design, identifying dynamical regions that govern system behavior or distinguish between qualitatively different modes is highly valuable. While the Lagrangian Coherent Structure (LCS) concept is widely established for analyzing dynamical systems and extends the notion of stable and unstable manifolds to time-varying systems, its application in three-dimensional astrodynamics remains restricted. This paper details a new technique developed by the authors, DA-LCS, which applies to astrodynamics using an E-Restricted Three-Body Problem as a case study. Direct construction of full 3D LCS structures for the Sun-Mars configuration is achieved from the variational LCS theory, even under numerically difficult initial conditions. Detailed analysis demonstrates how the LCS effectively segregates areas of distinct behaviors without relying on prior knowledge. Furthermore, researchers examine the impact of integration duration and initial condition parameterization on the resulting LCS. Key issues regarding floating-point arithmetic limits and their role in generating round-off errors during difficult simulations are highlighted, alongside practical strategies to address these challenges.

Visible thermal Re-identification (VT-ReID) struggles with significant inter-modality discrepancies alongside variations within the same identity. While distribution alignment addresses these issues, conventional methods typically only account for intra-identity variations. Addressing this, this paper introduces Cross-Modality Earth Mover's Distance (CM-EMD), a solution that mitigates intra-identity variation impacts specifically during the alignment of different modalities. CM-EMD employs an optimal transport framework that prioritizes weight assignment for sample pairs with lower within-identity variations, ensuring stronger modality alignment by concentrating effort on inter-modality discrepancy rather than diminishing returns on intra-identity changes. 

In addition to CM-EMD, two complementary strategies introduce significant advantages: Cross-Modality Discrimination Learning (CM-DL), which counters discrimination loss caused by feature shifts by optimizing the ratio of between-class to within-class variance, leads the network to capture more distinguishable features. Second, the Multi-Granularity Structure (MGS) facilitates comprehensive alignment by coordinating information at both coarse and fine details levels. Comprehensive evaluations confirm these methods, validating their effectiveness alongside state-of-the-art results on two VT-ReID benchmarks.

This master’s dissertation introduces an algorithm for the automated taxonomy of scientific literature employing deep learning, with a comparative analysis against established classification methods. In addition, the primary objective involves crafting a versatile application programming interface (API) that facilitates automation within existing software environments by integrating an actual proof-of-concept built upon a convolutional neural network. This REST-based classification system is proposed as the design foundation for the thesis. The work demonstrates that a deep learning approach delivers exceptional accuracy for multi-document category detection and successfully showcases the viability of incorporating such models into broader ecosystems through REST services.

Semiflexible filament networks are prevalent support mechanisms across biology, seen in everything from blood clots and bacterial biofilms to structural components in plant and animal tissues. However, our grasp of how specific architectural features relate to these networks' highly strain-sensitive mechanical properties remains limited. This study presents simulations of three-dimensional networks formed via an irreversible crosslinking process between linker-decorated semirigid filaments. We analyze structures resulting from a basic diffusion-controlled assembly and evaluate their rheological steady-state properties across a span of pre-strains that traverse the strain-stiffening transition area. The work establishes how network connectivity relies on the availability of crosslinkers and outlines this relationship as well as its role in both linear elasticity and nonlinear strain-stiffening behavior, drawing correlations between simulated results (linker-decorated networks) and prior experiment measurements of linker-concentration-based elasticity coefficients of actin gels.

While cyclic induction reasoning within the inductive first-order predicate fragment (FOIDL) remains decidable, the traditional verification technique requires an exponential-time complement operation on Büchi automata. We previously proposed a polynomial-checking approach, where the computationally heaviest stages involve comparisons analogous to multiset path orderings (MPO). We then detail our implementation of this strategy within the Cyclist theorem prover, named E-Cyclist. This version successfully validated all proofs present in the Cyclist distribution. Additionally, we introduced specific heuristics capable of automatically determining the MPO-based trace orders required for the soundness properties by analyzing proof derivation traces directly.

Representations serve as the foundation of the majority of deep learning systems, where a representation's effectiveness is directly linked to its ability to capture information regarding specific factors of variation. The quality of these representations is contingent on the learning algorithm employed and the nature of supervision used. We introduce a new technique utilizing weak supervision by partitioning data into groups based on certain invariant factors that remain common within each set. By identifying relationships between items across different partitions, our approach learns robust features inherent in active factors that vary throughout sets while discarding those that do not vary. Consequently, our method can effectively utilize both partially and completely unsupervised data—including information from disparate domains—because it focuses exclusively on active factors. We address the complex challenge of transferring synthetic-to-real object poses without relying on any pose annotations by extracting pose information at the category and cross-domain level. Furthermore, our approach is versatile: it can optimize supervised tasks by refining intermediate representations and operate in practical settings with scarce, set-labeled natural images, accommodating abundant nuisance variations.

We provide an extensive exploration into the existence and uniqueness of Lu's momentum map. Specifically, we define the infinitesimal momentum map and examine its characteristics. This investigation enables a description of reconstructing the momentum map from its infinitesimal counterpart. Additionally, we outline the conditions required to ensure the uniqueness of the momentum map.

Exact discrete symmetries, when realized non-linearly, effectively shield a theory from ultraviolet sensitivities. This framework allows quadratic divergences to vanish entirely and permits light scalar particles arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking to acquire mass while the symmetry itself remains intact—a stark contrast to non-linearly broken continuous symmetries, which rely on explicit breaking mechanisms to generate pseudo-Goldstone boson masses. These symmetry-stabilized masses and scattering amplitudes present significant opportunities for both theoretical advancement and the burgeoning experimental search for axion-like particles (ALPs). Utilizing the machinery of invariant theory and analyzing natural potential minima, we demonstrate that an abeliain or non-abelian subgroup of the original ultraviolet discrete symmetry usually persists explicitly within the spectrum ("Wigner realization"). This surviving symmetry serves as a distinct signature; its detection through the observation of two simultaneous degenerate scalars for abeliain cases or three for non-abelian ones, along with their specific multi-scalar production ratios, could reveal the parent ultraviolet discrete structure. To illustrate, we provide an in-depth examination using precise $A_4$ and $A_5$ symmetry models.

Although significant theoretical and observational progress has been made in tracing molecular magnetic clouds, their 3D morphology remains unresolved, necessitating multi-scale observations for a comprehensive understanding of star-forming magnetic environments. This study reconstructs the 3D magnetic morphology of the Perseus molecular cloud and contrasts it with theoretical formation model predictions, which expect filament clouds to exhibit bent magnetic fields. Using integrated data from line-of-sight observations combined with Galactic magnetic field and multi-wavelength surveys, alongside new data on the magnetic vector orientation relative to shock interactions and Galactic history, the full 3D field structure of the Perseus region is determined. Represented in the plane of the sky, the morphology appears as a longitude-transverse concave arc, consistent with both models. This study represents a unique achievement in 3D molecular magnetic reconstruction and suggests that cloud-forming fields maintain interaction memory. Ultimately, the 1st time such reconstruction has been accomplished demonstrates that the magnetic structures of the Perseus region are remarkably compatible with theoretical predictions regarding filament creation through shock interactions.

In these cooperative contexts, an agent must predict human movers' likely future states—for instance, basing this forecast on their teammates' historical behaviors—which becomes increasingly crucial. Human behavior driven by goals is intricate; it is layered, exhibits hierarchy, and operates simultaneously across many temporal granularities yet. Despite this well-established observation, there is relatively minimal scholarly commitment to adapting multiple-time-scale features for simulating these behaviors, which leads us to suggest that an LSTM network-based lattice might prove itself as valuable for this endeavor. Our paper suggests a proposal for an LSTM network structure capable for harness information from multiple-time-scale features for predicting future human actions while modelling human behaviour at various levels scales. Our method demonstrably outperforms other models that lack flexibility to account for temporal granularity when predicting human actor performance. Finally to verify our assertion, We assessed model efficacy by analyzing behaviour from a virtual environment designed using urban rescue simulations based in Minecraft to explore predictive capability under real-world constraints. Our architecture showed significant improvement by using temporal granule in task completion than non-grained or similar architectures.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has extensive utility in mobile environments; typically, foundation NLP models are fine-tuated in federated learning (FL) setups to handle diverse linguistic comprehension tasks. Currently, this approach necessitates hundreds of thousands of labeled data instances from mobile devices. However, because users often lack the desire or know-how to annotate data, this scarcity falls within the "few-shot" category—acting as a pivotal barrier to widespread mobile NLP adoption.

For the first time, this research explores the intersection of Federated Learning and NPL in few-shot scenarios, termed FedFSL. By combining advances in pseudo-labeling and prompt engineering, we constructed a training pipeline that achieves competitive accuracy even with a mere ~0.05% of the data (i.e., under 100 samples) being labeled, while utilizing unlabeled regions of the data as needed. To bring this into reality, we present the system FFNLP, which employs novel architectural designs to mitigate high computational overheads: (1) Curriculum pacing, which adaptively injects pseudo-labels aligned with learning progression; (2) Representationally diverse data filtering to generate pseudolabeling only for the most suitable candidates; and (3) Strategic planning that balances training iterations with model architecture depth. Collectively, these innovations cut down training latency by up to 46.0×, client energy consumption by 41.1×, and network traffic by approximately 3,060. These results demonstrate that Federated Learning is indeed viable even when only minor portions of the mobile training data are labeled.

We investigated video-specific autoencoders enabling users to explore, modify, and compress video data for transmission efficiently. Policymakers and professionals across diverse fields, including political science, frequently employ specialized, expert-designed hierarchies to interpret extensive datasets containing untagged information. We introduce HierSeed, an unprecedented weakly supervised methodology tailored for this objective. The algorithm operates efficiently in both computational resources and data consumption, assigning texts to specific topics by balancing document frequency metrics with the established hierarchical architecture of those topics. Employing recent observations, we have created multi-component equilibrium models for a Milky Way-like galaxy disk. These models utilize collisionless-gaseous numerical simulations, which simultaneously integrate the equations of motion for both collisionless particles (via direct gravitational integration) and gas (via Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics, SPH). After approximately one billion years, the simulations yield a substantial central bar extending about three kiloparsecs in semi-minor axis, accompanied by multi-armed spiral structures formed by combinations of two-, three-, and four-armed patterns. Both the bar and spiral configuration persist for at minimum three billion years throughout our computational run. The presence of this galactic bar restricts permissible spatial density profiles for Milky Way subsystems. specifically prohibiting the disk bar's emergence if the disk density scale length surpasses 2.6 kiloparsecs, and the phenomenon is also hindered by dense, compact central stellar bulges. Moreover, the observed peak in the central regions of Milky Way's rotation curve is accounted for by perturbations to the non-circular motions induced by the galactic bar.

Heterogeneous catalysts face significant image segmentation challenges due to their intricate surface and bulk structures, weak intrinsic tissue contrast, and often sparse dispersion of catalytic nanoparticles (NPs)—difficulties that current state-of-the-art deep learning methods struggle to overcome. To address these issues, we employed an artificial intelligence-based strategy to segment $\gamma$-Al2O3/Pt catalytic materials across multiple classes despite data imbalance. Our approach integrated the U-Net's fully convolutional backbone with a weighted focal loss function. Evaluation, based on the alignment between predictions and ground truth using Dice similarity (DSC), recall, precision, and Hausdorff distance (HD), confirmed the model's high accuracy. Specifically, the U-Net variant with weighted focal loss attained a mean DSC of 0.96 ± 0.003 for the $\gamma$-Al2O3 support and 0.84 ± 0.03 for Pt nanoparticle segmentation, with a boundary overlap error below 2 nm at the 90th percentile HD threshold for both classes. Our deep learning-assided automatic segmentation successfully generated high-resolution images of the relationship between the complex surface morphology and Pt nanoparticles by processing extensive high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) tomo datasets.

Task-adaptive pre-training (TAPT) addresses limitations in labelled data and boosts performance by fine-tuning unlabelled data for downstream applications; however, current adaptation methods largely rely on deterministic rules that struggle with generalisation. Solving underwater acoustic propagation relies heavily on the Normal Mode method, traditionally implemented via finite difference techniques or recently through spectral approaches for enhanced accuracy. This approach maps differential equations from physical space into spectral space utilizing orthogonal Chebyshev polynomials, resulting in a matrix eigenvalue/eigenvector system used to resolve horizontal wavenumbers and modal functions. Validation tests, comparing acoustic field calculations against classic benchmarks based on difference methods, demonstrate that the proposed Chebyshev-Tau method surpasses it in computational precision. Furthermore, performance analysis reveals that this technique operates faster than the Legendre-Galerkin spectral approach.

While this article addresses molecular simulation, its derived theoretical findings are applicable to all general overdamped Langevin dynamics simulations. Molecular simulations frequently assess system complex stability, such as that of ligand-receptor pairs, by calculating the expected duration the complex survives before dissociation. Dissociation in this context represents an "out" event as the process leaves a specific subset $ S $ within conformational state space. However, directly computing these exit transition rates for stochastic processes where such events occur infrequently proves difficult with standard simulation approaches. The challenge of identifying a low-variance computational procedure to derive statistics regarding these rare exits remains unsolved. Consider, for instance, a simulation modeling a diffusion process: as the time-dependent trajectory remains contained within $ S $, no useful information is gathered regarding these rare statistics. Data regarding the escape rate is accumulated solely when the process eventually exits $ S $. Yet, if $ S $ is a variable set (a fuzzy set defined by a membership function) allowing for nuances like being 'on the brink' of exit, this provides additional contextual cues. The central difficulty then arises: how should we mathematically define an exit transition rate specifically for exits derived from such a fuzzy set?

Perturbations confined to a real network can ignite system-wide cascade failures, thereby obstructing its overall operations. While conventional analytical methods predominantly rely on static frameworks like percolation or propagation limited strictly to first-neighbor links, these approaches often fail to model the distinct nonlocal dynamics inherent in actual cascades. To address this deficit, we present a dynamical model translating the failure spread into a self-avoiding random walk where nonlocal jumps toward still-functioning nodes occur with specific probabilities at each step. Although this process inherently lacks the Markov property, we successfully define the system's nonequilibrium critical behavior and the statistical distribution of the cascades' cessation times. Both numerical simulations on realistic and synthetic biological and transportation networks, alongside theoretical predictions, align perfectly. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively measures the vulnerability of complex, interlinked architectures to nonlocal cascade failures.

The quantum mechanical problem concerning a particle collapsing toward a central singular potential $U(r)$ remains fundamental, yet its resolution is currently incomplete. Existing results merely establish that if $U(r)$ diminishes sufficiently quickly as $r$ approaches zero, the energy spectrum of the Schrödinger equation lacks a lower bound. However, because the associated wave functions exhibit a singularity at $r = 0$, the limit of the ground state cannot exist. Consequently, spectral unboundedness alone serves as a necessary, but not conclusive, condition for collapse. To demonstrate actual particle descent to the center, an explicit wave function characterizing this process must be derived; achieved in this work, we obtain an exact solution to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for this scenario. We have explicitly calculated the specific phase collapse law marking the contraction of the wave function's localized region to a single point, along with the time-dependent profiles for the average kinetic and potential energies as well as the momentum of the falling particle. The analysis reveals that the known conditions deemed necessary for collapse are, under analysis, both simultaneously necessary and sufficient for the process to occur in reality. Recent interest has surged over the last few years regarding the application of Hamiltonian dynamics within deep learning environments. Serving as an inductive bias derived from physical principles, Hamiltonian dynamics offer neural networks the benefits of reliable long-term forecasting, enhanced interpretability, and efficient data usage. Conversely, these models impose constraints of energy conservation or dissipation on input data and entail increased computational costs. This paper delivers a comprehensive, methodology-focused survey of recent Hamiltonian neural network models. Initially, it highlights the principal contributions of these architectures and compares their performance across four interrelated dimensions: generalized Hamiltonian systems, symplectic integration, generalized input formulations, and extended problem contexts. Finally, the work outlines potential challenges and emerging avenues for development in this field.

Optical and optoelectronic matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) techniques have demonstrated significant potential to accelerate machine learning (ML) with remarkable speed. Integrating nanomaterials could further enhance performance due to their exceptional characteristics, yet inconsistencies and variations among nanostructures on macroscopic scales remain a major barrier to large-scale implementation. In this work, we introduce a novel optoelectronic architecture utilizing graphene-based photodetector arrays combined with spatial light modulators for MVM. The platform's ultrahigh carrier mobility in graphene, nearly zero power requirements for electro-optic control, and extreme parallelism indicate the feasibility of achieving both ultrafast data processing and ultralow power usage. Additionally, we establish a method capable of executing accurate calculations despite using imperfect components, paving the way for scalable systems. We further validated the flexibility and broad applicability of our approach by successfully running several representative ML algorithms, such as singular value decomposition, support vector machines, and deep neural networks.

Here we show how the overall upper estimate for the approximation is a little better for Sequential Bayesian Quadratic estimation processes than for the other approaches alone; however, some faster methods are actually better for all purposes because of linear scaling with an increasing quantity of selected samples. While most current Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) techniques primarily concentrate on generating extensive pseudo-training data to improve performance, very few tackle the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation. This study redefines various GEC environments as distinct tasks and introduces a methodology that applies few-shot meta-learning for domain adaptation entirely without synthetic pseudo data. By leveraging large data sets from source domains as anchors, we aim to create initial model parameters that enable rapid adaptation to new, low-resource target domains. Our approach specifically refines GEC capabilities across first languages (L1) acquired by learners developing non-native proficiency. Using nine diverse L1s as sources for meta-initialization and five additional L1s as target areas, we evaluate the system using an L1-specific adaptation corpus. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method achieves a 0.50 point higher F_0.5 score compared to multi-task transfer learning baselines and allows for effective mastery of new domains using as few as 200 paired training instances.

TabNet, which employs attention-based feature transforme rs and has proven effective on tabular inputs, served as our baseline. In contrast, we propose Fair-TabNet, which utilizes representation learning to separate predictive information from sensitive attributes. This architecture minimizes losses related to both non-attendance and sensitive variables simultaneously, ensuring that sensitive and prediction representations remain orthogonal during training. Experiments were conducted on a 2019 dataset containing 210,000 hospital appointments. Preliminary outcomes indicate that our Fair-TabNet approach outperforms TabNet in terms of prediction accuracy, fairness assurance, and convergence speed. Results when comparing Fair-TabNet with other state-of-the-art tabular models are also promising, though further performance enhancements can be achieved through improved hyper-parameter tuning.

Additionally, when individuals' disqualifiers comply with the consecutive ones property, {\sc{GCAI} proves tractable for both rule variations in terms of polynomial complexity. Finally, our W[2]-intractability proofs leverage methodologies that yield significant lower bounds concerning both exact solution algorithms and the size of problem kernels.

Current quantum computers lack the resources necessary to execute practical quantum algorithms. Deep ansätze often compromise viability in near-term devices by introducing trainability bottlenecks that degrade efficiency. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained widespread adoption for modeling graph-structured data due to their superior performance across various real-world tasks. Recently, knowledge distillation (KD) techniques for GNNs have facilitated notable advancements in both model compression and effective knowledge transfer. Nevertheless, the prevailing KD methods typically depend on extensive datasets of labeled examples from the target distribution—a constraint that lacks accessibility during deployment, especially when teacher models are trained on obscure or challenging datasets. Motivated to solve this limitation, this paper introduces DFAD-GNN, the first end-to-end framework capable of executing data-free adversarial knowledge distillation specifically tailored for graph data. DFAD-GNN leverages the generative-adversarial network paradigm by employing two adversary components as discriminators—the pre-existing teacher and a target student model—to guide the generator. Meanwhile, the generator synthesises new graph structures derived from the target distribution to provide supervisory signal for the transfer of knowledge from the expert to the subordinate model. Experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks using six significant graph benchmarks confirm that proposed method significantly surpasses existing SOTA for graph-based classification under the data free setting.

This study introduces a new approach to generating talking face videos exclusively from speech input. Techniques that convert speech into video show great potential in entertainment, customer service, and human-computer interaction sectors. Specifically, vocal elements like timbre, accent, and tempo hold rich cues related to a person's visual characteristics. A primary difficulty involves separating distinct visual attributes hidden within audio signals. Our proposed solution employs a lightweight, cross-modal distillation strategy designed to uncover disentangled emotional and identity data from unlabelled video data. These extracted features, combined via a generative adversarial network (GAN), are synthesized into realistic talking face video clips. By utilizing meticulously designed discriminators, the framework achieves highly realistic generation outcomes. Evaluations with real individuals reveal that our model isolates emotional expressions based solely on speech, resulting in spontaneous and natural facial movements. When compared to a baseline that requires a spoken audio track and a fixed static photograph, the generated output is virtually indiscernible for its static version. Furthermore, user studies confirm that our method surpasses current techniques in rendering emotion within synthesized videos.

Federated learning represents a novel approach in machine learning that conducts model training across independent, decentralized devices. A primary benefit of this method is the retention of raw training data on user devices, such as mobiles, ensuring only updated models are synchronised centrally. In the supervised setting, the responsibility for labelling typically falls to clients; however, obtaining these ground truth annotations is often unfeasible due to high costs and significant marginal error rates in specific applications, like human activity recognition. Consequently, vast quantities of unlabelled data go untouched. Predominant federated learning solutions, centred largely on supervised tasks, have overlooked this untapped unlabelled resource. Moreover, the viability of standard federated algorithms for self-supervised tasks and the handling of unlabelled data remains uncertain. Existing research that does address semi-supervised challenges generally assumes heterogeneous datasets. This work establishes a solid baseline for evaluating federated semi-supervised learning using distributed datasets. It details how conventional autoencoders and the Federated Averaging mechanism underperform when trying to learn robust features across real-world heterogeneous datasets. These discrepancies call for a deeper exploration into the capabilities that can help leverage the extensive homogeneous unlabelled data found in collaborative mobile environments more effectively than the current state-of-arts.

Rascal is a potent, high-level transformation language designed to streamline software language engineering tasks, including the definition of program syntax, program analysis, transformation, and code synthesis. The language incorporates essential features like native collections (lists, maps, sets), algebraic data structures, sophisticated backtracking-aware pattern matching, and multi-strategic high-level traversals. Because Rascal's features carry rich semantic complexity, understanding their interactions can be challenging. The documented formal semantics cover a significant subset of Rascal, known as Rascal Light, offering a well-structured foundation for creating formal methodologies such as static analysis frameworks and type systems. Furthermore, this work defines and formally verifies several crucial properties of these semantics, including the purity of its backtracking mechanism and strong typing, partial progress guarantees, and the existence of a terminating execution subset.

Current Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) approaches primarily rely on cross-modal reasoning over discrete viewpoints. However, these discrete schemes can stifle both numerical and spatial reasoning capabilities in agents due to partial object detection within single views and redundant observations across multiple views. A promising alternative involves projecting discrete views into a unified bird's-eye view capable of aggregating fragmented and duplicate data into a comprehensive context. Although existing metric maps offer the necessary coverage, their utility is diminished by restrictive semantics—such as fixed labels, usually ill-suited for the agent's vocabulary—and scalability limits hindering long-term language grounding and strategic planning. Drawing from advancements in robotics, our study introduces hybrid topo-metric maps into VLN frameworks, leveraging topological maps for long-range planning and metric maps for precise short-range reasoning. Beyond enhancing mapping capabilities through expressive deep features, we further propose a pre-training framework utilizing this hybrid representation to learn language-aware map semantics, a process that bolsters cross-modal grounding and ultimately improves language-guided navigation. Extensive evaluations on three major benchmarks confirm the efficacy of our route-based approach and establish a new state-of-the-art in VLN performance.

Generating dense depth maps solely from sparse LiDAR scans remains a formidable challenge. Although numerous depth-only techniques have emerged, they still lag considerably behind RGB-guided approaches that leverage additional color data. Our analysis reveals that current depth-only methods yield promising accuracy in "normal" regions where measurements are accurate, reasonably dense, and correctly distributed. Conversely, their performance deteriorates significantly in "overlap" regions (characterized by ambiguous boundaries between objects in cluttered scenes) and "blank" regions (completely lacking sensor readings), due to an absence of dependable input. Addressing this shortcoming, we introduce the Coupled U-Net (CU-Net), an effective architecture designed specifically for LiDAR-only completion. Departing from conventional large regression models, our approach pairs a local U-Net to derive precise values in well-defined areas, providing robust initialization for overlap and blank zones via two globally connected components. Ultimately, these outputs are consolidated using learned confidence heatmaps. We further integrate a confidence-driven outlier removal mechanism to filter unreliable predictions based on simple constraints. Experimental results on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that CU-Net outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods while maintaining computational efficiency through reduced parameters. Additionally, the method exhibits strong robustness across varying LiDAR sampling rates and diverse lighting and weather scenarios.

Initially, we introduce a (non-private) successive elimination algorithm for strictly optimal identification of this arm and prove that it achieves $\delta$-PAC boundaries, characterizing both necessary and sufficient sample complexities. We also establish an asymptotic lower bound on expected pulls, demonstrating that our method performs optimally modulo logarithmic factors; notably, our lower and upper complexity bounds rely on a novel suboptimality metric defined specifically for quantile problems, as the case where the gap converges to zero makes identification unfeasible for finite arms. Secondly, targeting private reward scenarios, we develop a differentially private successive elimination algorithm that guarantees a bounded, finite sample size even for distributions of unbounded support. Crucially, our algorithms are design-dependent-free, not requiring any prior knowledge of gap sizes or other specific statistical parameters of the environment.

In transport networks, individual users naturally select routes independently to reduce personal travel costs, often generating inefficient global results. Consequently, researchers have increasingly focused on road tolling strategies designed to recover these efficiency losses and align user behavior with system-optimal traffic patterns. Such strategies, however, typically require precise knowledge of travelers' attributes, such as origin-destination pairs and values of time, which are rarely available in actual applications. Motivated by real-world limitations, this work proposes an online learning method for setting network tolls to encourage heterogeneous users toward a system-efficient state. We present a streamlined and effective algorithm that updates tolls each time period using exclusively observed aggregate road flows, eliminating dependence on private traveler attributes and ensuring privacy protection. Assuming user trip pairs and values of time are drawn independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.), we prove the proposed approach achieves an expected cumulative regret and road capacity violation proportional to $ O(\sqrt{T}) $ over $ T $ periods; this regret is measured relative to an optimal offline oracle possessing complete user data. Further, we establish an $ O\{ \sqrt{T} } \} $ lower bound, demonstrating that our algorithm is optimal with respect to these constants. Empirical validation against benchmarks on a real-world traffic network underscores the superior performance of our approach and its practical relevance.

Furthermore, we note that intermediate magnetic fields significantly boost stability in an manner dependent on the equation of state, whereas strong magnetic fields dominate these distinctions, causing different state equations to exhibit nearly identical stability behaviors. Additionally, across all modeled equations of state, ambipolar diffusion was observed to act as a destabilizing agent on the filaments.

We established a theoretical framework linking quark-level topological diagrams with hadronic-level rescattering dynamics. Within this approach, both the standard triangular hadronic topologies and the intermediate topological-scattering diagrams—which serve as the bridge between the two—are mathematically represented in tensor form. The validity and comleteness of topological-scattering diagrams are confirmed through the analysis of quark substructure in meson-meson scattering. Each triangle diagram's coefficient can be extracted from its topological-scattering counterpart, ensuring the total rescattering amplitudes align with those predicted by chiral Lagrangians. Specifically, when only short-distance $T$ diagrams constitute the weak vertex in triangle diagrams, the rescattering contributions within diagrams $C$, $E$, and $P$ follow a fixed $SU(3)_F$ symmetry ratio of $L(C):L(E):L(P) = -2:1:1$. Conversely, rescattering contributions appearing solely in $T$ and $A$ diagrams originate exclusively from $SU(3)_F$ symmetry breaking. Using $D\to K\pi$ and $D\to \pi\pi$ decays as test cases, we detailed our methodology. Our results demonstrate that isospin relations for triangle diagrams hold in these decay modes, and conclusions regarding $D$ mesons under $SU(3)_F$ symmetry extend naturally to $B$ mesons under $SU(4)_F$.

Crowd counting remains a burdensome task due to the rigorous requirement of labeling every individual, prompting various semi-supervised methods designed to mitigate annotation costs. Typically operating under limited funding, these existing approaches focus on densely annotating all persons within only a selected subset of image data. While promising, our position is that this "None-or-All" methodology is suboptimal because the heavily labeled sections of each chosen crowd scene tend to be homogeneous, whereas numerous unused scenes may harbor highly diverse individual types. Consequently, this study aims to disrupt the prevailing labeling paradigm and pioneer the reduction of spatial labeling redundancy. Unlike prior art that annotates entire fields, our technique selectively identifies and labels only the representative instances; specifically, these are determined vertically and hormonaly and modeled as cluster centers via Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM). Furthermore, to maximize utility from the vast unlabeled data, our system exploits intra-image similarities among individuals to oversee unmarked regions through direct feature propagation rather than the error-prone label swapping used by former systems. This approach effectively channels redundant labeling signals caused by individual likenesses into useful supervisory inputs. Empirical results across mainstream benchmarks demonstrate that this strategy significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods by large margins.

Beyond improvements in computing velocity and storage capacity, methodological innovations have significantly enhanced stochastic simulation performance. This paper examines variance reduction in matrix computations using factorization techniques. It reviews established methods for reducing variability in estimating individual large matrix entries; while popular approaches ignore the variance reductions achieved through matrix factorization, we explain that obtaining a matrix square-root factorization in many key cases can lead to substantially superior stochastic performance. Furthermore, we introduce a factorized estimator for the trace of matrix products, which numerical experiments show is up a thousand times more efficient on specific problems regarding Gaussian process log-likelihood. Finally, we present a novel estimator for the log-determinant of positive semi-definite matrices to treat the determinant as a probability density's normalizer.

The low surface brightness (LSB) spiral UGC 8839 rarely exhibits stellar formation, with a notable exception being a massive HII region complex situated at its outermost disc edge. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this cluster, researchers compared new Hα images alongside archival photometric images of UGC 8839 against similar data for four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings indicate that the off-center star formation in UGC 8839 arises from a hyper-stable, dark matter-dominate disc; in this system, the stability limit exists solely when reaching a minimum in the outermost disc regions. Furthermore, by adopting an analytical framework robust against the challenges of low surface brightness objects and sparse statistics, the study determines that such complexes are not anomalous if the HII region luminosity follows a power law, implying the structure is native rather than a merged satellite. However, a distinct bias toward larger radii for HII regions in UGC 8839 was observed relative to those found in the comparison galaxies. UGC 8839 effectively illustrates the correlation between the dark-to-barionic mass ratio and disc stability. Finally, a three-body interaction—a smaller-scale counterpart to forces hypothesized behind the phenomenon in Malin 1—is proposed as the consistent explanation for the extreme outer disc star formation.

Significant advances have elucidated the computational abilities of spiking neural networks. Nevertheless, spiking remain more demanding than rate neurons because of the wide variation in time constants; spikes occur in much shorter durations compared to inter-spike intervals, both of which dwarf typical timescales for learning. Mathematically, these disparate timescales create a classic scenario of stiff problems. Furthermore, spiking networks present substantial obstacles to analytical study. A viable strategy to simplify them is to refine mean-field theoretical models by integrating information regarding spike correlation structures; ideally, such an augmented generalized activity model would consistently encapsulate both firing rates and inter-spike covariances. To achieve this, a rigorous framework for self-consistent spiking networks can be constructed and subjected to a perturbation analysis, treating a parameter such as the reciprocal neuron count as the small expansion factor. Under standard mean-field approximation, the description converges toward rate-like dynamics, while the initial terms in this first-order expansion effectively account for covariances.

Our work presents the XLM-R XL and XLM-R XXL architectures, two state-of-the-art masked models boasting 3.5B and 10.7B parameters respectively, designed to enhance cross-lingual language model performance. Notably, XLM-R XXL also edges out RoBERTa-Large by a margin of 0.3% average on English-based GLUE benchmarks while extending language coverage to 99 additional low-resource languages. These findings indicate that scaling pre-trained model parameters can effectively boost proficiency on well-resourced languages while delivering significant gains for those with fewer data points. We have made our trained weights, code, and methodology open-source for public access.

This article introduces Particle-based Object Manipulation (Prompt), a novel methodology for handling unfamiliar objects directly, eschewing the need for pre-derived 3D models or extensive pre-training on large datasets. At the core of Prompt lies a particle-based representation where each element encodes specific geometric, physical, and feature-level properties of an object point, along with its spatial relationship to other particles. Drawing parallels to model-based analytic techniques, this representation empowers robots to infer an object's geometry and dynamics to select effective manipulation actions akin to them. Conversely, it aligns with data-driven methods by acquiring this representation online in real time through visual sensing, specifically utilizing multi-view RGB imagery. Consequently, this approach bridges visual perception and robot control. By integrating the reasoning capabilities of model-based strategies with the flexibility of data-driven learning, demonstrably, our results show that Prompt adeptly manages diverse daily objects, including transparent ones, executing tasks such as grasping and pushing. Furthermore, our studies indicate that this method surpasses the leading state-of-the-art purely data-driven grasping techniques on everyday items, accomplishing these feats without any reliance on offline training data.

Various methodologies attempt to locate specialists by constructing expert listings presumed to reflect skill levels and assessing their performance using standard Information Retrieval (IR) metrics. Nevertheless, we determined that (i) expert listings often result in partial orders rather than full ones (partial ordering), (ii) lack completeness, (iii) and implicitly convey hierarchy instead of discrete ranks, which contrasts with how standard IR metrics function. To enhance this existing body of knowledge through formal IR adaptations, we propose crafting dedicated evaluation metrics for expert listings. This study focuses on a preliminary approach: implementing solutions addressing these deficiencies to contextualize expert listings, then analyzing IR measures using these tools to discern necessary refinements and persistent constraints. The findings reveal that our mitigation techniques render the vast majority of standard measures suitable for this broader context. Furthermore, while metrics based on precision and recall traditionally overlook ranking order, reinterpreting lists as sets of ordered pairs proves promising and offers significant utility. Conversely, cumulative metrics prioritize ordinal information but incur greater execution overhead, supporting a strategy that leverages precision-recall frameworks when correctly formatted.

Accordingly, this paper investigates and compares the per-device energy consumption of distributed edge inference across the four existing partitioning strategies. The objective of this analysis is to identify which specific strategies are most promising, and under what particular conditions, for lowering energy consumption at the edge during distributed CNN inference.

Temporal graphs, comprising timestamped, directed edges connecting various nodes, effectively represent diverse complex systems, including those in digital communications and financial markets. While temporal motifs generalize static subgraph patterns by accounting for edge sequences and durations, counting their occurrences is a critical yet challenging aspect of temporal network analysis. Current methodologies either fail to address temporal motifs adequately or struggle with efficiency, especially in dynamic stream processing environments where data arrives sequentially. Consequently, this study introduces approximate temporal motif counting strategies based on random sampling initially, starting with two offline algorithms that include a standard Edge Sampling (ES) method for broad applicability and a hybrid Improved Edge-Wedge Sampling (EWS) method tailored for three-node/three-episode motifs. We further develop the Streaming ES (SES) and Semi-streaming Edge-Wedge Sampling (SEWS) versions of these algorithms for real-time, incremental edge discovery. A thorough theoretical analysis validates the bounds and computational complexities, which inform extensive experimental testing on realistic datasets. These evaluations confirm that our offline algorithms, ES and EWS, offer superior accuracy, efficiency, and scalability compared to leading sampling techniques. Furthermore, the adaptive SES and SEWS variants deliver up to three-order-of-magnitude performance gains over their offline counterparts while maintaining comparable precision for temporal streams.

Masked annotations for medical images—particularly 3D volumes—often serve as a significant barrier in creating dependable machine learning models. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the user-guided domain adaptation (UGDA) framework, which leverages prediction-based adversarial domain adaptation (PADA) to represent the joint distribution of mask predictions and user inputs within a unified model. By anchoring the process with these interactions, UGDA directs and aligns the mask predictions accordingly. A key advantage of this approach is its capacity to utilize both labeled data for learning semantics from unlabeled instances alongside an understanding of the high-level intent behind various UI representations. We evaluate UGDA on the task of segmenting pathologic liver organs using a clinically diverse cohort of 927 patient scans. When relying solely on extreme-point UIs, UGDA achieves a segmentation mean accuracy of 96.1% (14.9% for worst-case performance) on average, surpassing the Deep Extreme Points (DEXTR) method's scores of 93.0% average to 89.8%. Notably, even when presented with a fraction of the available user interaction data, the model maintains this superior performance by minimizing user effort and delivering robust, state-of-the-art segmentation reliability.
