This paper introduces a new method for performing few-shot semantic segmentation using only sparse labeled images, particularly effective for the medical domain where sparse labeling significantly reduces dataset annotation expenses. Built upon Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), our approach leverages sparse labels during the meta-training phase and dense labels for evaluation in the meta-testing phase, enabling models to infer dense masks from limited training data. Our experimental assessments utilized four Chest X-Ray datasets to evaluate both grid-based and point-style annotations. Findings indicate that our approach is uniquely robust when the target and source domain tasks differ substantially; despite utilizing annotations covering less than 20% of a target image's pixels in few-shot settings, our model delivers Jaccard scores competitive with fully dense-labeled scenarios.

The explosive increase in network traffic generates vast dataset volumes. Manually labeling such data to identify intrusions is cumbersome and susceptible to errors. Additionally, traffic characteristics involve intricate non-linear, time-dependent relationships. Existing state-of-the-art detection methods rely on hybrid supervised models using correlated feature subsets. However, these approaches typically entail high computational demands, require manual model fine-tuning, and depend on data labeling, all of which impede real-time processing performance. While unsupervised methods can reduce computational load and the need for labeled data, a majority fail to account for spatio-temporal dependencies found in traffic. To mitigate this, we propose a unified Autoencoder that integrates Multi-Scale Convolutional Neural Networks with Long Short-Term Memory architectures for network traffic anomaly detection. Specifically, our Multiscale Convolutional Neural Network Autoencoder first analyzes the dataset's spatial properties; subsequently, the resulting latent space representation is refined using an LSTM-based Autoencoder to process temporal features. To enhance accuracy, the framework integrates two Isolation Forest methods to rectify false positives and negatives. Our proposed method achieves a notable performance advantage and outperforms traditional unsupervised models along with existing contemporary solutions when evaluated against the NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and CICDDoS2019 datasets.

Future MeV-scale neutrino experiments are well-positioned for using a Compton scattering detector (CSD) capable of reconstructing both the energy and direction of charged particles. One favorable option involves a novel target material, slow liquid scintillator (SlowLS), which disentangers Cherenkov light from scintillation light for detection. A multi-ton CSD was simulated using a Geant4-based tool to model micro-scale phenomena involving particles, photons, and readout electronics, including photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) and associated hardware. Parametric variations of the SlowLS samples were simulated to test a diverse range of scintillation yields and time-constant characteristics. Utilizing a thorough understanding of the underlying signal mechanisms, predictive models were derived to estimate PMT charge and temporal data, enabling efficient reconstruction of the energy, trajectory, and positioning of incident particles. This study outlines the reconstruction performance—assessing resolutions in energy, angle, and location alongside particle identification (PID) capabilities—and analyzes performance dependencies on light yield and timing constants within these specific scenarios. These insights will serve as critical design guidance and a performance benchmarking foundation for next-generation MeV-scale CSDs utilizing SlowLS.

This paper presents predictions of Arctic Ocean sea surface salinity (SSS) leveraging satellite measurements. Since SSS serves as a key proxy for detecting Arctic shifts, these predictions provide vital context for climate change dynamics. A primary focus is on water masses erroneously categorized as ice by satellites, a common challenge in ocean monitoring. Traditional retrieval methods employ conservative ice masks to handle salinity data near ice, often leading to significant information loss; however, our goal is to generate plausible SSS values for these regions. Doing so not only offers a more comprehensive view of the Arctic's SSS surface but also supports future applications requiring high-resolution data near ice boundaries or coastlines. To achieve this with extensive satellite records and the Arctic's intricate geography, we introduce BORA-GP (Barrier Overlap-Removal Acyclic directed graph Gaussian Processes), classifying a set of scalable nonstationary processes capable of managing complex domains. BORA-GP builds sparse directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where neighbors adhere to specific barriers and boundaries, effectively characterizing dependence in such constrained environments. Consequently, BORA-GP yields more reasonable SSS estimates where direct observations are absent and delivers superior performance in simulations within various constrained zones compared to leading models. Paleo-detectors represent a proposed experimental method for searching for dark matter that diverges from the conventional use of tonne-scale instruments to observe nuclear recoils in real time. Instead, paleo-detectors analyze small volumes of naturally occurring deeply underground rock (at depths greater than 5 km), capturing nuclear damage tracks from recoiling nuclei over geological timescales ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr). Contemporary microscopy techniques are increasingly capable of detecting these nanometer-resolution tracks within macroscopic rock formations. By leveraging such extreme integration periods ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ Gyr) in combination with low keV-level energy thresholds and 100 kilotonne-year exposures, paleo-detectors could investigate dark matter-nucleon interaction cross-sections orders of magnitude below current limits established by traditional direct detection experiments. In the following analysis, we refine these sensitivity projections using enhanced background models and updated spectral analysis methods. Furthermore, our results underscore the forecast's resilience to uncertainties regarding sample age determining, unmeasured background parameters, potential systematic errors in modeling background spectral shapes, and mineral radiopurity. Even under conservative conditions where sample concentrations are up to $10^{-8}$ in weight—surpassing expected radiopurity standards of ultramafic igneous or ancient evaporate rocks—paleo-detectors could theoretically probe sub-eexisting DM constraints. Specifically, for dark matter masses below 10 GeV/$c^2$, this technique could theoretically access sensitivity down to the conventional neutrino floor typically associated with xenon-based detectors.

In this paper we present a recent, understudied framework for event detection (ED), recasting the challenge as a question-answering task that accommodates multiple responses and leverages entity support. As quantum many-body simulators evolve, Hamiltonian tomography has emerged as a critical verification tool for quantum devices. We examine methods for retrieving the Hamiltonians of two-spin chains, specifically those exhibiting 2-local and 3-local interactions, by analyzing local observables. Our findings demonstrate that once both system models attain a specific critical length and exhibit a certain thermal steady state, the local Hamiltonian can be reconstructed solely from this state using the homogeneous operator equation (HOE)—as introduced in Reference [1]. To elucidate why such a critical threshold exists and as an auxiliary recovery strategy, we introduce an alternative approach based on solving energy eigenvalue equations (EEE). Utilization of this EEE method yields a complete numerical agreement with the original HOE results. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical equivalence between the HOE and EEE approaches. Specifically, by applying the EEE framework to analyze the HOE constraint system, we derive an analytical formula for the rank of its constraint matrix; this expression provides a general criterion for accurately defining the required critical bond length across all scenarios.

Providing rational justification for a data point involves selecting specific features that highlight its abnormality compared to typical data, a critical step in supporting downstream decision-making. We introduce a novel Sum-Product Network (SPN) based method to resolve this issue. Capitalizing on the efficient marginal inference supported by these probabilistic graphical models, we can generate outlier scores directly for selected subsets rather than from scratch. This shift from standard forward beam search allows for the implementation of backwards elimination; this backward selection is arguably robust against omitting critical features in complex high-dimensional spaces but relies on less redundant search processes to be effective. We are empirically validating that this SPN approach yields state-of-the-art performance, surpassing both contemporary heuristic-heavy search techniques and modern approaches based on deep machine learning.

Machine learning models developed using unfiltered data often inadvertently harm data from underrepresented demographics. In response, we tackle the challenge of constructing learning datasets in real-time to develop classifiers that achieve fairness within a minimax framework. Our approach first presents an adaptive sampling strategy grounded in the optimism principle, accompanied by theoretical performance guarantees. Building on this, we introduce heuristic modifications of the method designed to scale effectively with large, practical applications. Instead, RG iterations evolve toward two specific destinations: a "cubic" fixed point or a transition driven first by fluctuations. These paths represent separate universality classes differentiated by the symmetry of the resulting ordered states. We demonstrate that trigonal or tetragon-performing perovskites fall respectively into one of these dual classes.

The observation of a single perceived universality class stems merely from the proximity of the isotropic fixed points to that in a stable configuration. For example, before shifting into a first-order phase transition, such exponents in tetragon-type cases can retain "isotropic" characteristics. We suggest specific new experiments to validate these hypotheses. Furthermore, similar splitting of these universality classes is anticipated in any scenario where two or more fixed points compete in their stability.

We investigate lepton flavor violating (LFV) B meson decays within a general two Higgs doublet model featuring sub-TeV exotic scalars by examining two distinct theoretical regions. In the first scenario, where dynamics are driven by a dominant additional top Yukawa coupling $\rho_{tt}$, standard flavor constraints such as $\ell \to \ell^\prime \gamma$ and $h \to \ell \ell'$ indicate that rates for LFV B decays remain well beyond current detection limits. The quest to resolve the black hole information paradox offers a critical test for candidate quantum gravity frameworks. String theory has advanced in solving this puzzle through the development of the "fuzzball" and microstate geometry models. These approaches argue uniquely on the basis of string theory to account for black hole structure, asserting that horizons and singularities arise only because other theories lack sufficient degrees of freedom to capture underlying physics accurately. Consequently, fuzzballs and microstate geometries re-conceptualize black holes as horizon-less and free of singularity within the string theoretic paradigm, solving not just the paradox but revealing the hidden microscopic details of these objects. This text outlines that specific viewpoint, reviews its current development stage, and highlights promising future discoveries on the verge within these insights.

The study analyzes how local Quantum Dephasing Protocols affect the Loschmidt echo system, a metric highly responsive to the integrability of background dynamics. In integrable systems, such as the Heisenberg model, the Loschmidt echo is sensitive to the parameters associated with the protocol operator as well as the specific QDP occurrence moment. While incoherent QDPs occurring at larger intervals allow for a greater probability of system revival to its initial state, coherent QDPs consistently result in some loss of this restoration probability. Conversely, non-integrable cases, exemplified by the kicked Harper model, display a characteristic decay when compared with integrable counterparts. This decay tends to be slower when the underlying classical Hamiltonian lacks chaos, and in general, the Loschmidt echo successfully differentiates between integrable and non-integrable dynamical regimes during QDP events.

The marginal ice zone represents the fluctuating boundary between consolidated pack ice and the open sea, where ocean gravity waves control the region’s boundaries and properties, thereby mediating atmospheric-ocean-ice exchange and ice movement. Over the last ten years, pivotal experimental efforts have provided critical data on wave evolution in this area; while significant knowledge gaps persist, these findings have fueled substantial progress in understanding the region’s influence on the global climate system. Presently, we present three-dimensional, motion-based vessel imaging of wave dynamics alongside concurrent measurements of floe dimensions, findings which promise to significantly expand existing marginal ice datasets. Our images, detailing direction-frequency spectra for waves, are integrated with concurrent wind speed data and reanalysis products to expose the intricate multi-faceted composition of cyclonically driven wind-and-swells and quantify trends in the development of high-amplitude waves traveling across sea ice.

Global pulsar timing arrays have recently disseminated results from their search for a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal; though definitive proof in current timing residuals is still lacking, a statistically significant detection is anticipated through future data accumulation with enhanced quality. Stochastic algorithms are typically employed to sample vast parameter spaces during data inference. In this study, we aim to eliminate effects caused by the inherent stochasticity of sampling within the inference framework. We evaluate contrasting nested sampler configurations against the widely utilized Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method regarding both parameter sampling for pulsar timing arrays on the same datasets and computational efficiency. While parameters derived from various algorithms align consistently, we advocate for the use of two distinct samplers for future data analyses. This approach facilitates robustness through robustness checking and enables cross-validation between methods, ensuring realistic execution times alongside rigorous inference.

This paper introduces Fast Motion Deblurring-Conditional GAN (FMD-cGAN), a solution designed for blind motion deblurring of a single image that yields superior structural similarity and visual appearance. Like many deep neural networks, GANs struggle with large parameter counts and high computational demands, making deployment on resource-constrained devices like mobile units and robots challenging. To address this, we integrate a MobileNet architecture featuring depthwise separable convolutions to minimize model size and inference time without compromising output quality; specifically, the model size is decreased by a factor between 3x and 60x compared to the nearest competitors. The final lightweight Deblurring cGAN not only processes images faster than its closest rivals but also achieves qualitative and quantitative results that exceed those of various state-of-the-art blind motion deblurring methods, enabling effective real-time application as demonstrated by our current experiments on standard datasets.

Although considerable research investment has occurred into learning-based methods for industrial assembly over the past few years, widespread adoption remains stagnant in industry. This text attributes that failure not to inherent algorithmic limits, but to the prohibitively large design space associated with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), emphasizing that bridging the gap requires adopting a discipline-specific, industrial-oriented paradigm distinct from academic norms. This paper establishes specific criteria for industry-focused DRL and applies them to benchmark an approach using "demonstration against demonstrations" against solutions created by a leading industrial integrator, utilizing the newly established NIST assembly standard. By evaluating these choices, we demonstrated how several years of dedicated investigation enabled our DRL system to surpass the baseline integrator consistently in both speed and reliability. Furthermore, we present competitive trials involving a human operator completing high-dynamic, randomly moving insertion challenges. Our results suggest that DRL not only exceeds traditional engineered methods and even human dexterity in specific tasks, yet room remains for progress; additional demonstrations are available at https://sites.google.com/view/shield-nist.

We propose a beta mixture model to detect significant connections between $P predictors, even when $P $ is very large. This approach applies principles derived from convex geometry to regulate the false discovery rate for edge estimation in graphical networks. The `betaMix` method makes no specific assumptions regarding the overall network topology and does not presume that the graph structure is sparse. The findings and conclusions from our work apply broadly to numerous data distributions, encompassing those that follow spherical symmetry, ranging from both light-tailed and heavy-tailed variants.

Shear strain localization within shear bands links velocity-weakening instabilities to earthquake occurrences. This study simulates the stead-state planar shear of numerical granular material (simulated gouge) constrained between parallel boundaries. Testing both fixed stress and constant shear-rate conditions reveals that each boundary type produces unique velocity profiles and resulting frictional laws. While the inertial number, denoted as $I$, primarily dictates the behavior of these granular layers, conditions of constant shear stress also reveal specific dependencies involving normal stress and layer thickness. Crucially, shear-band localization, which marks the quasistatic regime ($I<10^{-3}$) during rate-controlled experiments, disappears entirely in stress-controlled loading. Conversely, under stress control, flow terminates when the macroscopic coefficient of friction reaches the quasistatic friction limit. A shear regime emerging at higher $I$ values (inertial domain, specifically $I>10^{-3}$) characterizes a distributed mode of shear featuring a resistance that strengthens as shear rate increases, alongside rising porosity, explaining the dynamic mechanism behind shear under constant shear stress conditions. Rationally based on reduced fluctuations in shear forces at grain contacts during stress-controlled loading, direct observation of porosity both within and outside shear bands provides a physical explanation for why the switch from quasinestationary and localized shear movement correlates perfectly with the switch to inertial behavior with distributed strain.

We introduce a generalization of a conductor-like concept for numerical semigroups and extend it to higher dimensions by defining a corner element for these generalized structures. Furthermore, the properties of our new definition and its interactions with documented invariants, alongside an algorithm to identify all semigroups sharing a specific corner, are examined. Finally, establish lower and upper limits on the count of hyperplane numerical semigroups for a fixed point in a corner.

Stratifications combined with iterative differential equations serve as the positive-characteristic equivalents of complex linear differential equations; however, explicit examples of such stratifications remain limited. The primary objective of this work is to establish stratifications on both projective and affine curves within settings of positive character and to identify the corresponding differential Galois groups. Additionally, the study offer partial solutions to the "differential Abhyankar conjecture," thereby enriching the available literature. The methodology relies on $p$-adic and rigid analytic techniques, leveraging the properties of Mumford curves and their associated Mumford groups. By constructing regular singular stratifications through these tools, the paper generates a wealth of new differential Gailois groups and provides specific insights regarding the tame fundamental groups of affine curves, making explicit examples for previously unstudied curves, as well known mathematical concepts regarding the Galian group's differential relations to the existence of explicit examples for various strataifications.

We introduce a novel approach to lane detection and segmentation utilizing generative networks, contrasting with traditional methods that rely on discriminative models to classify pixels by semantics. By training a generative adversarial network to model the probability distribution of lanes and road symbols, our framework generates context-specific road features for input images based on this distribution, using subsequent quantization to determine the nearest class labels. Tested against the state-of-the art on four datasets, BDD100K and two variants of the Baidu ApolloScape datasets, the methodology outperforms existing techniques and demonstrates greater robustness in degraded conditions due to enhanced capability in detecting faded lines through occlusions.

We offer a comprehensive 3D resistive MHD physical analysis of jet generation in circum-stellar disks within binary systems, examining local and global system dynamics including angular momentum transfer as well as accretion and ejection mass rates. Unlike previous research, this study incorporates a complete magnetic torque alongside an outflow, vertical angular momentum transport due to motion, and binary torques. Our analysis examines the system's distinct 3D morphology within the context of tidal forces, identifying a novel feature where disk-induced spiral patterns evolve into and launch the outflow, which we term the {\em jet spiral wall}. This newly named {\it spiral} walls structure exhibits specific temporal characteristics, with the outflow lagging slightly behind the disk spiral. Our results highlight the critical significance of vertical angular momentum transport and magnetic torque in the system's angular momentum balance even in binaries. While gravity-driven torque originating from a time-dependent 3D Roche potential serves as the fundamental driver for most observed 3D phenomena, contributions from $\phi$-derivatives of magnetic pressure ($\phi$-terms) and $B_{\phi}B_r$ stresses remain minor. Additionally, data indicates that a binary environment enhances the disk accretion rate by roughly $20$% and boosts the disk wind mass flux by $50$%.

Achieving consensus among robots in a swarm remains a foundational issue in the field since it investigates whether group members can agree. Recently, the "contamination" problem introduced a new dimension to this challenge, requiring robots to reach an agreement despite adversarial entities actively trying to sway them toward a conflicting consensus. This paper seeks a consensus algorithm under contamination conditions using a high-level approach: converting the problem into a centralized two-player game where each participant controls specific robots in the swarm and attempts to steer the whole system toward their own desired value. We defined a performance metric for each participant, demonstrated its direct link to winning probability, formulated the globally optimal game strategy, but proved its impossibility in distributed environments due to the complex nature of swarm interactions. Consequently, the study analyzes the problem on a streamlined model, comparing global superiority through simulated evidence against locally optimal tactics.

Utilizing techniques from finite free probability to interpret matrix processes involving eigenvalues, standard, and generalized singular values of random matrices, we adopt remarkably elementary models anchored exclusively in the analysis of expected characteristic polynomials. Although several of our findings coincide with existing results in random matrix theory, our principal contribution—pertaining to generalized singularvalues—appears broader than the canonical models (Hermite, Laguerre, or Jacobi) traditionally recognized. Validation through a sequence of simulations reveals that this novel process can manifest unique behaviors absent in standard models, yet our methods still capture these occurrences effectively. Since we are equipped to calculate identical statistics for this innovative model as for established ones, future exploration into this area appears both promising and worthwhile.

To achieve this adaptability, we developed the hierarchical human-robot learning framework (hHRL), an autonomous system comprising five distinct controllers—disclosure, promise-making, instruction, feedback, and inquiry—governing a central algorithm that employs machine reinforcement learning (or meta-controls) to tailor challenge levels and feedback to a learner's unique progression patterns, facilitated through long-intervention evaluations over 3+ months with 5- to7+ year-olds. Additionally: sustained user engagement levels were maintained throughout the study and families deemed these systems adaptable and beneficial. Ultimately, autonomous personalized SAR systems offer feasibility along with real-world viability for chronic in-home therapeutic assistance of learners requiring diverse forms developmental interaction or instruction adjustments across time periods within domestic spaces or natural environments.

This study examines the challenge of model estimation and reward-free learning within episodic Block MDPs, where decision-makers observe rich contexts derived from a limited set of latent variables. We first establish a lower bound on the information-theoretic error rate for estimating the mapping from observations to latent states and propose an algorithm that achieves this theoretical limit; using this same method, the complete structure of the MDP is also recovered to achieve a similar optimal theoretical guarantee while ensuring convergence in large samples. We subsequently explore policy learning under a framework without rewards and demonstrate how an optimal near-optimal policy can be recovered using the proposed model, achieving both efficiency and rate optimality relative to accumulated samples. This article presents an analysis of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sea surface images utilizing a Radon domain formulation to enhance linear features, which aids the accurate detection of ship wakes. This study provides two findings regarding uniform confidence intervals designed for the extreme quantile and the tail index. Initially, it demonstrates that creating a confidence interval that is both length-optimized and uniformly correct over a local non-parametric family of tail distributions is infeasible. Salient object detection in optical remote sensing images (RSI-SOD) proves highly challenging primarily because of variations in scale and form and the unpredictable nature of object positions in these views. While existing SOD algorithms perform adequately on natural scenes, they struggle to adapt to remote sensing images without addressing their specific complexity. This paper introduces the Attention-Guided Network (AGNet), developed expressly to tackle SOD tasks in these domains. The framework consists of two main components: a Position Enhancement Stage, and an Enhanced Detail Refinement Stage. Within the former, a Semantic Attention module operating alongside a Contextual Attention module collectively identifies object locations with high accuracy. The latter leverages a self-refinement unit to gradually enhance segmentation outputs by integrating bidirectional attention and reverse-attention mechanisms to sharpen detailed structures. Further boosting performance from image, voxel-wise, and distributional perspectives, the model incorporates a Hybrid loss strategy, supervised to refine outputs at multiple levels of hierarchy. Thorough evaluations on prominent benchmarks demonstrate the AGNet's robust performance and state-of-the-art competitive standing compared to other methodologies. The implementation is scheduled to be open-sourced at https://github.com/NuaaYH/AGNet.

Gaussian Process (GP)-based surrogate models possess the inherent ability to address anomalies stemming from sparse, missing, or inconsistent data within the digital twin modeling and simulation framework, particularly for Accident Tolerant Fuel (ATF) concepts. This chapter examines the MFK method and illustrates its application using thermal conductivity measurement datasets for ATFs, demonstrating its superior capability compared to traditional Kriging with minimal data. The resulting MFK mathematical models facilitate straightforward integration with subsequent uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analyses for both fundamental research and broader product development. Ultimately, the chapter highlights the potential of MFK-based surrogates as components integrated into digital twin systems for ATFs.

This study introduces an innovative framework for proactively forecasting traffic flow bandwidth to overcome a critical flaw in current network management: the temporal lag between generating operational decisions and executing their countermeasures when network conditions change. By ingesting raw real-world traffic packets and transforming them into feature-enriched streams, the approach employs trained machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forest, Deep Neural Networks, XGBoost, and Decision Trees, to predict bandwidth consumption for the next interval at the flow level. Feeding these forward-looking estimates to the management system, rather than relying on immediate bandwidth figures, enables more precise, future-aware state-based decisions. Validation across a dataset of nearly one million flows and 15 distinct time window configurations (spanning 0.03s to 4s) revealed that Random Forest outperforms both rival models in reliability and accuracy, improving results with over 19% reduction in mean absolute error and 18% in root mean square error. Consequently, the experimental outcomes suggest this method can equip network management systems with the ability to make significantly more enlightened administrative choices through predicted states.

Notably, this intersection appears increasingly relevant in research focusing on compositional semantics. Furthermore, empirical evidence suggests that merging both methods can address their inherent limitations, despite theoretical gaps in formulating how they should work together in tandem.

**Context**: Educating software engineers necessitates a robust and practical foundation in empirical research methods to support the industry's reliance on real-world evidence. Typically, students encounter their final, most applicable instance of such training within their master's thesis.

**Challenge**: Collaborating with industry for thesis work mandates a delicate equilibrium between academic interests and practitioner needs. While achieving high-impact empirical results is possible, it remains difficult to do so within a standard thesis timeline, often causing academic rigour to decline when practical industrial value is the primary goal. Despite methods like Design Science Research (DSR) existing to support this, students consistently find these frameworks difficult to implement effectively in thesis settings.

**Proposed Solution**: Design Science Research offers a mechanism to balance academic inquiry requirements with design-oriented outputs; however, little literature exists on operationalizing DSR successfully within a master's thesis format involving industry partnership. To address this gap, we integrate practical guidance and field experience into existing DSR frameworks. This resource offers pragmatic advice for university and industry stakeholders—specifically examiners, students, supervisors, and researchers—to streamline the process of conducting design science theses.

**Methodology**: Utilising DSR, we analyzed twelve design science theses completed in the preceding seven years. This analysis examined common pitfalls and effective practices derived from student-supervisor interactions, supervisor-industry relationships, examiner feedback, and reviews of publications arising from this work.

**Outcome**: We deliver actionable recommendations on framing research inquiries, organizing thesis documentation, and orchestrating empirical work collaboratively with industry professionals.

Inferring accurate road maps directly from aerial and satellite imagery remains a longstanding technical hurdle. These advancements pave the way for real-time road detection on embedded systems even during airborne flights.

Although researchers have advocated for using deep learning to establish links between natural language items, such as requirements and bug reports, and source code, current approaches often suffer from limited efficiency during execution and a shortage of labeled data. The framework is applied to retrace connections between code commits and user issues within Open Source projects. Topic taxonomies capture the underlying organizational structure of document corporas and hold significant value for diverse applications ranging from web search to information filtering. While recent years have seen the rise of unsupervised methods for automatically deriving these taxonomies from raw text data, creating an accurate taxonomy from zero prior knowledge presents a major challenge. This paper investigates strategies to overcome this hurdle by using available partial topic structure as guiding cues to infer the complete hierarchy, proposing a new framework titled TaxoCom for completing topic taxonomies. TaxoCom achieves recursive expansion of the taxonomy via novel techniques that cluster terms and documents into fresh subtopics. To distinguish new topics within a hierarchical context, its design tightly integrates embedding strategies with clustering logic by: (i) creating embeddings via a locality-based discriminative method to differentiate among known subtopics, which guides a novelty-aware clustering step to assign terms as candidates for establishment. Extensive evaluations across two realistic datasets reveal that TaxoCom not only produces high-quality taxonomies characterized by superior coherence and coverage but also surpasses existing baselines in a downstream performance metric.

The isovector axial form factor of the nucleon serves a central function in analyzing results from long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments. Consequently, the resulting parametrization—covering spacelike virtualities up to $0.7\,{\rm GeV}^2$ and featuring robustly quantified uncertainties, demonstrates excellent consistency findings of earlier lattice studies. This study introduces a decomposition framework designed to generate efficient feasible solutions for security-constrained alternating-current optimal power flow (SCACOPF) at an industrial scale, adhering to stringent real-time constraints. The proposed method complements the prevailing reliance on bounding the problem using convex relaxations. Developing in response to ARPA-E's Grid Optimization Competition's first challenge, the approach addresses a near real-time formulation of SCACOPF. This formulation involves optimizing a base case operating profile capable of surviving various single-element contingencies, followed by an adaptive re-adjustment of the system according to automatic frequency drop controllers and voltage regulators. The core methodology utilizes advanced nonlinear programming algorithms, incorporating nonconvex relaxations for complementarity conditions. Additionally, it features a tailored two-stage decomposition strategy employing sparse recursion term approximations, alongside rigorous contingency pre-screening and prioritization. The implementation highlights key technical advantages, including rapid model and derivative evaluations, robust warm-start capabilities, and asynchronous processing. Results from the independent ARPA-E benchmark for the Grid Optimization challenge indicate that the approach reliably delivers high-quality solutions across diverse network configurations and levels of complexity. The conclusion presents directions for extending and refining this methodology.

This work constructs a robust and highly precise numerical framework for solving the three-dimensional coupled Stokes-Darcy system. Employed is a Dirichlet-Neumann type decomposition, which iteratively resolves the domain by addressing Stokes and Darcy sub-problems with the associated interface conditions split across separating surfaces. Second-order boundary integral equations are derived for each component, where smoothing techniques are applied to the kernels to ensure boundary accuracy without sacrificing numerical stability. These integrals are discretized utilizing simple quadrature methods, which maintain high fidelity near singular boundaries. Tests involving flow of a viscous fluid around a porous Sphere with established analytical solutions yield converged, accurate results and delineate the iterative scheme’s behavior with respect to parameters. Validation extends beyond these specific cases, addressing general surface geometries, with outcomes confirming the scheme’s effectiveness and sensitivity.

Stellaar binaries are common stellar systems and play a key role among youth systems in forming architectures around many protoplanetary discs. We highlight the role of binary systems' coplanar or perpendicular orientations within circumbinary environments in making non axisymmetric disturbances on dust/gases distribution. HD 169142 inner protoplanetary disc was used to illustrate this, in which we suggest that the structure could come from a combinatious influence of binary and disk orbits within the binary system-planet configuration. Specifically, a mass ratio of 0.1, 9 au separation, slightly eccentric, and 90 degrees inclined secondary star with an orbiting Jupiter mass planet in a circular orbit reproduced dust rings at 13 astronomical units observed in scattered light. We predict how future monitoring over twenty years could test the dynamical changes caused by these orbits through changes in dust arrangements.

Global public health remains significantly concerned by water resource contamination stemming from pathogenic microorganisms of human origin. Routine monitoring typically focuses surveillance on just one or a select few microorganism species. However, establishing feasible periodic monitoring protocols and managing exposure risks demands trusted statistical methods for analyzing the interdependencies between microbial concentrations. Furthermore, since pathogens often exist in minimal numbers, many occurrences fall below detection limits, resulting in pairwise left-censored data that hinders accurate calculation of correlation coefficients. Consequently, improving the imputation of undetected values reduces correlation estimation errors. Our study addresses this by leveraging auxiliary information and developing an **asymmetric Tobit model**; an enhancement to the traditional Tobit model that effectively incorporates domain expertise when fitting censored data yields superior imputation results, a capability validated through empirical analysis.

We focus on identifying trojans and backdoors within deep neural networks. Consequently, we localize such trigger neurons from unpolluted inputs using counterfactual attribution and systematically excite them to detect shifts in model accuracy. A deep set encoder then processes the resulting data structure to facilitate robust Trojan detection regardless of model class counts or architectural variations. Implemented in the TrinityAI tool, our approach capitalizes on shared principles to address challenges regarding interpretability resilience and trust within deep learning paradigms. This work combines theoretical modeling and experimental measurements to investigate pressure-induced switching in the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) of the triangular antiferromagnetic compound Mn$_3$Sn. Our model indicates that compressive pressure significantly splits the in-plane Mn bond lengths—an effective trimerization—that modifies inter-plane exchange interactions to stabilize a helical antiferromagnetic ground state. Experimentally, the AHE in Mn$_3$Sn declines from 5 $\mu\Omega$ cm at ambient conditions to zero under approximately 1.5 GPa of pressure. Additionally, pressure-dependent magnetization data show a systematic evolution of the ground state from conventional triangular antiferromagnetism to the helical antiferromagnetic phase, a symmetry that suppresses the necessary Berry curvature for finite AHE. X-ray diffraction results rule out a structural phase transition as the cause of this effect, and ambient pressure measurements reveal a deviation in the temperature dependence of the in-plane lattice parameter under entering the helical phase, further validating proposed mechanism involving trimerization. Ultimately, the findings offer significant insights into stabilizing diverse magnetic ground states in Mn$_3$Sn and related systems with potential applications for AHE switching.

This study investigates the task of extracting generalizable re-identification (re-ID) features from video sequences without labels. To achieve this, we introduce two primary advances: first, Cycle Association (CycAs), a lightweight and scalable self-supervised method that ensures re-ID features are learned with efficiency proportional to the number of elements involved; and second, the release of LMP-video, a massive unlabeled dataset curated specifically for this purpose for training purposes itself. CycAs operates by enforcing a temporal cycle consistency constraint across consecutive video frames to extract re-ID features, allowing the model to be scaled efficiently across datasets with a linear computational overhead regarding data quantity. Meanwhile, the new extensive LMP-video corpus features 50 million unlabeled person crops sourced from over 10,000 YouTube videos; it offers the necessary volume to support effective self-supervised learning. Our experiments demonstrate that CycAs, trained exclusively with this dataset, learns robust representations capable of generalizing seamlessly to unseen domains and often achieves performance comparable to or exceeding state-of-the-art methods with labeled supervision by enforcing a no-label approach. Our work introduces three key developments: first, a tailored diffusion process for decoding scenarios; second, a neural decoder conditioned explicitly on the number of parity errors found in each step; and third, a segment-based search technique using syndrome information to optimize the backward diffusion step magnitude. By leveraging the strength diffusion models bring to ECC, the proposed method delivers leading-edge accuracy—surpassing other neural decoders by significant margins even with just a single reversal iteration.

Leveraging rapid advancements in Internet of Things (IoT) technology, low-earth orbit (LEO) satellite IoT architectures are anticipated to support wide-area coverage, massive connectivity, and energy-efficient IoT applications. In alignment with this vision, this study introduces a grant-free random access (GF-RA) solution specific to LEO satellite IoT, which operates without necessitating changes to the existing transceivers. Instead, it converts the received signal into a format suitable for tensor decomposition, utilizing its structural advantages to engineer a joint algorithm for active device detection and simultaneous channel estimation through Bayesian learning methods. Adaptive first-order optimization techniques, such as \textsc{Adam}, have revolutionized machine learning by scaling learning rates element-wise based on second-moment estimates of gradients, thereby accelerating the training of contemporary deep neural networks. However, these methods typically underperform compared to Stochastic Gradient Descent (\textsc{SGD}) regarding generalization and are prone to becoming stuck in local minima during the early training phases. Our analysis reveals that replacing the standard gradient within Adam's raw second-moment calculation with its momentum-enhanced counterpart successfully alleviates this limitation. This stems from the insight that momentum-weighted gradients provide superior directional information, making them a better choice for adaptive learning rate scaling than raw gradients. Consequently, we introduce \textsc{AdaMomentum}, an optimizer designed to combine rapid convergence with significantly enhanced generalization. To substantiate these results, we establish theoretical foundations for generalization improvements and offer convergence guarantees applicable to both convex and nonconvex problems. Large-scale experimental evaluations across various architectures and tasks confirm that \textsc{AdaMomentum} not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also maintains superior training stability.

Computer vision employs motion analysis to comprehend how moving entities behave across sequential images. To accurately analyze dynamic biological systems with both efficiency and precision, it is crucial to optimize motion tracking and develop effective representations for high-dimensional motion paths, facilitating prediction tasks. This detailed motion model was then inputted into a supervised denoising autoencoder named *4DSurvival*. This hybrid network incorporates an autoencoder learning task-specific latent representations trained on observed outcomes, producing a latent space optimized for survival prognosis. To accommodate right-censored survival data, the system utilized a Cox partial likelihood loss. In an evaluation involving 302 patients, our method significantly outperformed the human benchmark (C = 0.52, 95% CI: 0,53-0,65), achieving a higher prognostic accuracy of C=0.73 (95% CI: 0,68–0,78) with a statistical difference (p < 0,0001). These results validate an approach to efficiently predicting patient survival in computer vision tasks utilizing high-dimensional medical imagery.

As a prototypical antiferromagnetic system displaying multiferroic properties, hexagonal YMnO$_3$ shows ferroelectric and magnetic phase transitions at distinct temperatures via resonant magnetic diffraction. Identifying gravitational wave signals resulting from stellar-mass microlensing within the LIGO--Virgo frequency band remains difficult because such signatures are inherently faint. Nevertheless, these lenses are typically hosted within their galaxies, making microlensing events concurrent with strong lensing. This context suggests that analyzing events which exhibit both strong and microlensing features could notably refine our estimates of the weaker microlensing components. This paper presents a conceptual demonstration of utilizing parameter estimation data from a strongly lensed signal to bolster the inference of its microlensed counterpart, specifically using established Bayesian inference methodologies in gravitational wave studies. Ultimately, we anticipate this approach will substantially upgrade future capabilities to discern subtle imprints from stellar objects in gravitational waveforms produced by merging compact binaries.

The study of energetic particles' phase-space distribution is gaining significant traction, primarily because it offers a richer data set than conventional bulk metrics. By applying the Field-Particle Correlation (FPC) method and employing various techniques for solving the plasma kinetic equation, we investigated how oblique collisionless shocks energize ions. This comprehensive phase-space approach allows us to isolate distinct groups of energized ions. A primary objective was identifying specific ion demographics that reflect repeatedly off the shock front via shock-drift acceleration and utilizing the FPC method to differentiate these sub-populations within phase space. Additionally, we expanded our analysis to simulate complex three-dimensional shocks featuring dynamics like shock ripples, thereby validating that FPC successfully detects the corresponding energization signatures in broader system contexts. Consequently, this research broadens the previous uses of FPC to realistic collisionless shock environments, providing compelling validation of its efficacy as a tool for analyzing simulations, laboratory experiments, and spacecraft data.

This research paper addresses generalizable, perception-driven robotic manipulation specifically designed for high-precision tasks involving complex physical interactions. We introduce a closed-loop framework capable of managing a range of object instances without needing prior specific knowledge or extensive visual training, effectively managing significant differences within a single object category in terms of geometry, dimensions, and visual appearance. While existing methods typically integrate feedback loops based solely on fixed 6-DOF state estimations—which fail to account for substantial shape variations using static templates—we adopt an orientation-augmented kepoint-based approach originally developed for category-level pick-and placement. Extending this to our closed-loop system for contact-rich environments, we incorporate rotational orientation data to create a novel, action centric scheme. Instead of controlling standard operators, our system regulates the linear or angular velocities and forces applied specifically at the oriented keypoints through contact-driven feedback, thereby achieving a highly flexible approach. Experimental results show this framework successfully handles tasks with tight tolerance and high precision across shape and size variations. Finally, because the proposed representation relies heavily on object intrinsic properties rather than initial conditions or specific grasp geometries, we ensure a smooth, adaptable implementation.

Multiple-objective optimization (MOO), defined as the simultaneous optimization of conflicting goals, holds significance in machine learning, including reducing classification error and managing fairness across diverse populations. Given that optimal balance invariably implies that optimizing one metric compromises another, stakeholders must evaluate the Pareto frontier to select an ideal solution. This paper targets computational efficiency in locating the Pareto frontier: recognizing that generating the frontier from zero using stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMGD) is costly when training extensive neural networks on vast datasets, we introduce a predictor-corrector framework that explores the frontier as a manifold starting from limited initial solutions. State-of-the-art image captioning models typically rely on Region-based features because they supply crucial object-level insights essential for describing image content; commonly, these are generated by detectors like Faster R-CNN. Yet, they present several challenges, including limited contextual information, potential detection errors, and high computational costs. Adding grid-based features can mitigate the first two problems, but determining how to extract and combine both data types remains undefined. This paper introduces GRIT (Grid- and Region-based Image captioning Transformer), a Transformer-exclusive architecture designed to leverage both visual modalities for superior captions. GRIT substitutes the traditional CNN-based detector with a DETR variant for faster inference. Furthermore, its entirely monolithicTransformer architecture facilitates end-to-end training. This novel configuration, paired with the dual-feature integration approach, yields marked performance gains. Benchmarks confirm that GRIT surpasses prior methodologies in both inference speed and accuracy.

Car abductions constitute among the most significant offenses across numerous urban areas. Consequently, drivers navigating South Africa must maintain constant alertness to avoid becoming victims of this menace. This study focuses on creating a heatmap of hijack locations in cities by harnessing data derived from Twitter platform activity. Data processing begins by collecting posts tagged with or referencing the keyword "hijacking" within a selected city context: Cape Town. To filter relevant content for analysis, the following machine learning methodologies are employed: 1) Multi-layer Feed Forward Neural Networks (MLFFN); 2) Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN); and 3) BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). Evaluation through rigorous training and assessment phases revealed that CNN delivered peak performance, achieving an accuracy rate of 99.66%, compared to MLFFN and BERT, which scored 98.99% and 73.99% respectively. CNN also demonstrated superior metrics across Precision, Recall, and F1-score. Consequently, CNN serves as the tool for extracting relevant tweet data. These generated records are then visualized on a geographic dot map highlighting points within the City of Cape Town. Although current implementation utilizes a modest sample size consisting of 426 tweets, future phases plan to investigate evolutionary computation strategies to optimize the deep learning models. Additionally, a dedicated mobile application is currently being developed to render this spatial data accessible to the broader public.

Unlike earlier complex multi-stage strategies, this work introduces an end-to-end semi-supervised framework for object detection where gradual improvements in pseudo-label quality during a curvicular process eventually enhance detection training. Within this structure, we implement two efficient mechanisms: a soft teacher approach that weights the classification loss of every unlabeled bounding box according to the teacher network's score, and box jittering to choose robust pseudo-labels for regression training. Evaluated on the COCO benchmark, this method exceeds prior techniques across various labeling rates (1\%, 5\%, and 10\%), demonstrating strong performance even with abundant labeled data. Notably, applying 123K COCO images to full-training baselines increases a detector from 40.9 to 44.5 mAP (+3.6), while boosting a state-of-the-art Swin Transformer from 58.9 to 60.4 mAP (+1.5 detection and +1.2 instance segmentation). Finally, by combining the model with Object365 pre-training, detection accuracy climbs to 61.3 and instance segmentation to 53.0 mAP, establishing a new state-of-the-art.

Terahertz (THz) communications are recognized as pivotal enablers for integrated sensing and high-precision localization in sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks. In 6G paradigms, localization is no longer a mere side effect but a necessary component location-aware communications. To advance this vision and explore the associated challenges and requirements, this review examines the historical evolution of localization techniques alongside their current objectives and constraints in traditional systems. It subsequently details state-of-the-art progress in THz communications, including specific THz channel and system models. The study further formulates THz localization and sensing by framing them within 3D position/orientation estimation, covering geometry-based approaches and potential extensions. It also covers the design stages from offline planning to online optimization, presenting numerical simulation results and concluding with an outlook on research directions and key findings for the future. Preliminary data indicates that, when matching millimeter wave terms for transmission power and array size, THz localization delivers superior results. Indeed, equivalent localization performance in both regimes can either be cheaper via lower power consumption at THz or compact utilization through a smaller array footprint.

We introduce an end-to-end automated framework that jointly infers camera intrinsics, ground planes, and interpersonal physical distances from standalone RGB images or videos captured via a fixed viewpoint observing a 3D scene. By incorporating human pose priors, we propose an innovative direct method for pose-based auto-calibration and distance estimation, achieving the highest performance to date on existing public benchmarks. This solution allows standard camera arrays to measure real-world distances without relying on manual calibration or dedicated range sensors, making it suitable for diverse applications including social distancing and occupational safety. Additionally, we release MEVADA—a new global benchmark that extends the public MEVA dataset with detailed distance annotations—to support evaluation and foster future advancements in pose-based auto-calibration and distance estimation tasks.

This study lays the foundation for the formal discipline of Software Engineering, revealing key connections between it and Information Technology. Our inquiry drew upon a comprehensive analysis of leading journals, including *IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering*, *ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology*, the journal of *Automated Software Engineering*, the conference proceedings of *ICSE*, along with other significant publications, addressing central research questions. The work examined existing frameworks to articulate the necessity of software engineering within academic contexts, while successfully distinguishing it from computer science. Ultimately, these efforts advance our comprehension of how insights from Information Technology can bolster the development of software engineering as a rigorous academic discipline.

We introduce a collection of data-driven strategies designed to optimize machine learning performance on quantum information tasks. Focusing specifically on how to strategically construct training sets to boost the precision of unmodified neural networks in quantum state reconstruction, our approach demonstrates that rather than aligning training distributions exactly with the target scenario to achieve peak performance, it yields better results to intentionally overrepresent mixed states. This improvement stems from the differing degrees of constraint among states of various purities, which implies that networks should train primarily on the most variable (least constrained) states given a fixed data volume. To clarify these concepts, we present a simplified model that reveals the risks training synthetic data brings, specifically illustrating how hidden variables can harm performance, yet showing how a small amount of contrasting examples can successfully mitigate this degradation.

We introduce a method for Offset-free Model Predictive Control (MPC) that leverages model-plant mismatch learning. By integrating learned mismatches directly, the scheme capitalizes on the strengths while mitigating the weaknesses of both data-driven techniques and classical model-based approaches. Within this framework, we approximate the steady-state model-plant mismatch map using a General Regression Neural Network, constructed from historical data for various setpoints. While the learned map yields equilibrium mismatch estimates, it fails to capture dynamics occurring during transient periods; furthermore, inherent mismatches may fluctuate as system characteristics evolve during operation. To address this, we augment the model mismatch with a supplementary disturbance variable derived from a disturbance estimator within a standard nomination offset-free MPC structure. Integrating this compensation strategy into the finite-horizon optimization of MPC enhances both trajectory prediction and closed-loop performance. This integration effectively combines detailed mismatch knowledge with the robust stability guarantees of conventional estimator approaches, achieving an efficient compensation mechanism that simulation results validate. Finally, we extend the analysis of this proposed offset-free MPC framework to address robust asymptotic stability—a challenge often left unexplored in nominal counterparts—utilizing the acquired mismatch information for the stability proofs.

We introduce Xenon, an automated technique for formally certifying constant-time execution within Verilog hardware. By leveraging a novel framework that generates constant-time counterexamples, Xenon significantly reduces the manual effort required to identify root causes of verification bugs; it subsequently utilizes these examples to automatically produce minimal secrecy assumptions. Through its combination of assumption generation and modular reasoning, we demonstrate the ability to verify various circuits, including AES and a complex, highly modular AES-256 implementation that achieves a six-fold verification speedup (reducing runtime from six hours under 30), as well as ScarV, an obliquely robust timing-channel-hardened RISC-V microcontroller exceeding the size of prior verified designs by an order of magnitude.

Defects inherent to YBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{7-\delta}$ (YBCO) thin films induce a vortex arrangement resembling a glass, causing resistance vanishing even at near-zero current densities. These vortical lines are entangled and exhibit a signature scaling in isothermal voltage-current relationships. In contrast, randomly placed columnar fragment these entanglement networks to create a vortex Bose glass state. In the study reported below, we demonstrate the formation of an order-disordered Bose glass in a YBCO thin film incorporating a hexagonal lattice of 30 nm columnar defects. This regular pinning structure was precisely achieved using a 30 keV He$^+$ focused beam generated by a helium-ion microscope (FIB).

Scene understanding presents a significant challenge within computer vision, necessitating that every pixel within an image be classified. While traditional methods utilized color-based, manually engineered features, recent breakthroughs are attributed to deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which automatically learn hierarchical feature sets and have set new benchmarks. Typically, existing CNN approaches rely on separate post-processing modules, like superpixels, to finalize labeling decisions. This paper introduces a new architecture integrating CNNs with CNN-based transposal (DeepRCNN). Our trials reveal that deconvolutional CNNs uncover complex image structures beyond simple edges, surpassing the limitations of standard CNNs. We pair these capabilities with "multi-patch training," a method introduced here to extract spatial relationships between scene fragments. This integrated approach sets a new state-of-the-art record across four key benchmarks—Stanford 20B/SC, CSU04+SIFT, CMViD, and SceneNN/KITTI—while offering a fully automated, end-to-end training process that eliminates the need for additional post-processing steps.

The behavior of a suspended system under diverse static or oscillatory external fields is strongly determined by the equilibrium electric double layer encircling the colloidal particles. Conventional mean-field theories, specifically the Poisson-Boltzmann framework applied to salt-free suspensions, can be enhanced by integrating ignored factors such as non-uniform size variations and the ordered orientation of water dipoles. Our proposed model, which accounts for these factors, offers significant potential; it accurately predicts specific phenomena, notably a substantial drop in the suspension's relative permittivity and the formation of counterion strata near highly charged particles. In this study, we numerically determined the electric potential, counterion concentration, and relative permittivity surrounding a charged particle within a concentrated, salt-free suspension, correcting the calculations for non-uniform sizes and water dipole ordering. Findings underscore the value of such corrections for colloidal charges ranging from medium to high across all particle volume fractions, with the conclusion that including these effects is essential for advancing new theoretical frameworks to examine non-equilibrium properties in dense colloidal systems.

Medical image segmentation is commonly used to delineate structures such as organs and lesions. While current state-of-the-art techniques rely on deep learning for automated analysis, they typically suffer from limitations associated with supervised learning. This dependence on vast datasets that have been manually labeled by clinicians imposes significant effort on medical practitioners. The primary objective of unsupervised and semi-supervised segmentation strategies is to drastically curb the requirements for annotated data, thus lightening the clinical load. In pursuit of this, TricycleGAN represents an original network architecture designed for unsupervised and semi-supervised segmentation of medical imagery. The method employs three generator networks to perform translations between raw inputs and segmentation outputs via intermediate edge map predictions. In contrast to generative methods that depend on texture and color statistics, TricycleGAN relies on shape prior information, rendering it especially effective for applications where standard visual signals are unreliable or non-existent, such as ultrasonography. Preliminary evaluations of the TricycleGAN model are presented using clinical ultrasound data of kidney images as well as the ISIC 2018 benchmark skin lesion dataset.

This work introduces a robust metric for characterizing unidirectional emission in microcavity lasers. While Shannon entropy applied to far-field distributions—calculated within polar coordinates to ascertain directional symmetry and its stability against parameter-induced deformationsoffers superior performance compared to conventional methods—a phenomenologically defined divergence angle based on full width at half maximum (FWHM) often falters when analyzing structures with multiple peaks. In contrast, Shannon entropy applied to the Cartesian semi-marginal probability of far-field profiles achieves comparable results for standard cases but uniquely provides reliability for emitting profiles featuring complicated peak structures.

OTFS modulation offers the promise of robust communication in highly dynamic environments. However, estimating channels for this scheme is resource-intensive, as the needed pilot signaling scales proportionally with peak delay-Doppler spreads. This burden exacerbates drastically in massive MIMO contexts, where it also grows linearly with antenna count since delay, Doppler shift, and angle-of-arrival/departure correlation directly correspond to user and scatterer distance, velocity, and orientation. Motivated by this correlation to environmental geometry and motion metrics, we propose harnessing radar sensing capabilities to acquire this user and environment data. This acquired information will be integrated as an assistance tool for improving channel accuracy in both OTFS-based massive MIMO scenarios and radar sensing. As illustrated, treating the OTFS channel problem as one parameter estimation, and employing radar sensing elements such amplitude and phase, effectively restores the sparse matrix support (i.e., the active location in time and frequency; this paper formulates it in sparse optimization methods). Our developed algorithm is assessed robustly against state of practice 2D signal simulation set ups with existing communication data. Our results show that radar information enhances the accuracy recovery of sparse recovery algorithms over standard methods and leads to substantial reduction of OTFS-based channel feedback requirements, suggesting we have a new direction by integrating radar capabilities.

This study evaluates, to first post-Minskowksian order, one-loop corrections for the scalar-tensor gravitational effective potential involving a quartic scalar field self-interaction. Within the model, this effectively described theory predicts strong field regime instabilities that can extend an exponentially large region depending on the model parameters; potential applications for inflationary model scenarios and regions the model might enter during slow-roll.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) serve as a powerful framework for learning techniques by leveraging relationships embedded within structured graph data. Since Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects information onto eigenspaces and shares methodological similarities with the convolutional filters in GNNs, we introduce the Covariance Neural Network (VNN), a novel architecture adapted to process sample covariance matrices viewed as graphs. This paper provides a theoretical proof demonstrating that VNNs exhibit stability when subjected to covariance matrix perturbations, offering a significant improvement over traditional PCA-based methods, which are inherently unstable due to sensitivity in handling principal components with close eigenvalues. Experimental validation on real-world datasets confirms these theoretical claims, showing superior stability in VNNs compared to statistical counterparts relying on PCA. Furthermore, results from multi-resolution experiments reveal that VNNs support the transferability of performance across covariance matrices of varying dimensions—a capability unattainable through standard PCA approaches.

By embedding dual theories into an enlarged unphysical Hilbert space separated by entanglement cuts, this work investigates the entanglement structure of $\mathbf{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory in $2+1$ dimensions. The study confirms Li and Haldane's conjecture while establishing consistency between the entanglement Hamiltonian and the Bisognano-Wichmann theorem. In examining post-quench non-equilibrium dynamics, the research outlines the thermalization process for $\mathbf{Z}_2$ gauge theory through four distinct stages: initially, the maximization of Schmid rank coupled with the early-stage spreading of level repulsion; secondly, intermediate-time evolution exhibiting self-similar scaling with coefficients $\alpha = 0.8 \pm 0.2$ and $ \beta = 0.0 \pm 0.1$; and finally, the thermal saturation of von Neumann entropy.

Ground-truth datasets are standard in the evaluation and auditing of AI algorithms used for high-risk applications yet lack widely ratified quality benchmarks to measure the reliability of those labels. New empirical evidence demonstrates that label integrity can substantially skew outcomes in real-world algorithmic audits. Research using data labelers commonly hired by AI firms in India shows that even a high degree of label fidelity can falsely suggest performance disparities in Automatic Speech Recognition systems between urban and rural groups. However, these group disparities vanish after conducting an exhaustive and costly process of label cleansing. These findings underscore how the balancing act between data quality and annotation costs presents practical difficulties in conducting audits. Consequently, there is a pressing need to establish standardized milestones for label quality that achieve broad consensus.

Electrical manipulation of magnons facilitates novel pathways for information transport and logical device operation. In magnetoelectric multiferroic systems, this control relies critically on the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction, making its role fundamental. We utilized density functional theory to identify the source and quantify the magnitude of this converse spin-current DM interaction within the $R3c$ bulk phase of the multiferroic $BiFe_{1}O{}_{5}$. The findings confirm the presence of solely a single DM contribution arising from the spin-current model. Furthermore, by analyzing magnon dispersion across the entire Brillouin zone, we demonstrate that while exchange remains isotropic, both the DM interaction and anisotropy favor specific orientations for propagation and magnetization confined to the (111) plane. This study underscores the pivotal role of the asymmetrical potential generated by spin-current dominance over structural asymmetries derived from the anionic octahedral framework in multiferroic materials like $BiFe{}_{1}O{}_{5}$.

We investigate the finite blocklength performance within the moderate deviation regime concerning asymptotic information processing, where communication rates approach capacity thresholds concurrently with vanishing error. Precise characterizations of this error-cost tradeoff are derived for several fully Quantum communication protocols, such as quantum source compression, state recovery, entanglement-assisted channel coding, and channel simulation under entanglement assistance. A pivotal contribution of this work is an established rigorous link between the partially smoothed max-entropy and the hypothesis testing relative entropy; leveraging this relationship, we deduce the asymptotic expansion of partially smoothed max-entropy relative to independent, and identically distributed (i.i.d.) states within moderate deviation frameworks.

Finding minimal routes in a network is a fundamental graph analysis challenge vital for numerous resource routing applications. Malicious actors possessing the ability to alter graph structures can exploit this to distort traffic flows and profit from them. Addressing this threat in the Force Path Cut Problem, we investigate an adversarial attack where specific links are removed to force a targeted path between terminal vertices into the status of being shorter. Although we establish the computational inapproximability (APX-hard) for this scenario, we introduce an efficient polynomial-time algorithm dubbed "PATHATTACK," delivering logarithmic-factor approximations of optimal decisions. Broadening the inquiry further to Force Node Cut and Force Edge Cut, we focus manipulations aimed individually at nodes, with formulations in nonconvex optimization techniques offering heuristic solutions through internal use of PARTATHATCH as an oracle component. To illustrate the utility, we apply various algorithms across multiple synthetic and real networks highlighting the diverse set of systems that can best be exploited.

This paper introduces a multi-state adaptation of the recently formulated FDE-dab method, available in the Serenity program. The updated framework generalizes the initial method to couple any number of charge-localized quasi-diabatic states, facilitating calculations of both ground and excited-state spin-density maps as well as excitational energies. The results demonstrate that this approach achieves accuracy comparable to correlated wave function techniques such as Complete Active Space Self-Consistent Field (CASSCF) while significantly reducing computational demands. Furthermore, we detail several approximate computational strategies that not only lower the overall computational cost further but also systematically converge to the full FDE-dab solution. The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics focuses on the interplay between rapidly shifting demography and concurrent trait mutations, which drive the emergence of novel system behaviors. This emphasis on swift changes stems from extensive evidence of contemporary evolution found in laboratory settings and natural environments, exemplified by Trinidadian guppies. We argue that limiting this scope restricts a comprehensive synthesis of ecology and evolution. Instead, we maintain that emerging behaviors occur regardless of tempo, also manifesting in processes that unfold over millennia, such as interactions between riverine geomorphology and plant adaptation. By incorporating these longer-term feedbacks and landscape-level processes, we significantly broaden the realm of eco-evolutionary theory. Crucially, we contend that eco-evolutionary pathways remain dynamic and adaptable rather than static; specifically, factors like temperature and mutational sensitivity modulate ecological and evolutionary rates, causing them either to sync or fall out of step. We speculate that accelerated global change may increase the frequency of fast eco-evolutionary cycles and emergent system dynamics, thereby posing significant predictive hurdles for the scientific community. This review aims to forge a multidisciplinary framework integrating genomics with landscape science across diverse temporal scales, ranging from immediate shifts to deep evolutionary history.

Graph partitioning serves as a critical mechanism for distributing workload across multiple processors to minimize communication overhead and balance processing, its importance magnifying as applications migrate towards emerging accelerator-based supercomputers as standard hardware architectures. Currently, however, a distributed-memory, multi-GPU graph partitioner optimized for such parallel environments is unavailable. To fill this gap, we developed Spectral graph partitioner or Sphynx, which is built on the Trilinos framework's portable, accelerator-friendly stack, enabling the use of various preconditioners with a focus on their distinct strengths. This project applies Sphynx to systematically assess algorithmic options in spectral partitioning specifically for GPU performance across two categories of graph structures: regular (such as mesh matrices from finite element methods) and highly structured (such as social network data and complex web graphs), demonstrating the necessity for distinct configuration settings and preconditioners for each class despite recent performance declines from other methods. Experimental results on the Summit supercomputer reveal that performance improves with the use of this balanced load-balanced distributed-memory GPU parallel graph partitioner. When compared on the same platform, performance improves significantly for irregular graphs compared to parmetis mesh in finite element analysis which prioritizes accuracy. Under single-gpu testing on the nim-graph tool, it also provides a more robust balance and higher quality partition across a broader range when applied to any given problem.

In contrast to this letter-specific deletion, we introduce a more robust model, the "generalized circular one-way jumping finite automaton" (gcOJAFAs), which allows for the elimination of arbitrary subwords instead and functions cyclically on its input.
